lessons.title: Nigerian state capitals: four capitals required by the Week 1 assessment (outside scheme row 1)
objectives: Identify the capital of Lagos State.
Identify the capitals of Ebonyi, Plateau and Ogun States.
Match each of the four states to its correct capital.
lessons.body:
NIGERIAN STATE CAPITALS — FOUR ITEMS REQUIRED BY THE WEEK 1 ASSESSMENT

SUPPLEMENT STATUS
This is a small, original assessment-support supplement. It is deliberately labelled OUTSIDE SCHEME ROW 1 because the First Term Week 1 scheme row lists meaning, nature, scope and value of Geography, but does not include Nigerian state capitals. The source nevertheless asks for the capital of Lagos State in the General Evaluation and the capitals of Ebonyi, Plateau and Ogun States in the Theory question. This supplement teaches only those four capitals; it does not expand the scheme to all 36 states.

THE FOUR STATE–CAPITAL PAIRS

1. Lagos State — Ikeja.
2. Ebonyi State — Abakaliki.
3. Plateau State — Jos.
4. Ogun State — Abeokuta.

HOW TO STUDY THEM
Read each state name and say its capital aloud. Then cover the right-hand side and try to recall the capital. Remember that Lagos is a state and Ikeja is its capital; Abuja is the Federal Capital Territory, not the capital of Lagos State.

PRACTICE AND ANSWERS

Question 1 (4 marks): Write the capital of each state:
(a) Lagos
(b) Ebonyi
(c) Plateau
(d) Ogun

Answer:
(a) Ikeja
(b) Abakaliki
(c) Jos
(d) Abeokuta

Marking guide (4 marks total):
- Ikeja for Lagos — 1 mark.
- Abakaliki for Ebonyi — 1 mark.
- Jos for Plateau — 1 mark.
- Abeokuta for Ogun — 1 mark.

Question 2 (4 marks): Match each state to its capital:
Lagos; Ebonyi; Plateau; Ogun.
Options: Abeokuta; Ikeja; Jos; Abakaliki.

Answer: Lagos–Ikeja; Ebonyi–Abakaliki; Plateau–Jos; Ogun–Abeokuta.

Marking guide (4 marks total): award 1 mark for each correct state–capital pair. No half marks are needed.

SOURCE NOTE
The four capital pairs are checked against the National Bureau of Statistics' Nigeria map/table (Lagos–Ikeja, Ebonyi–Abakaliki, Ogun–Abeokuta) and the Independent National Electoral Commission's State Offices directory (Ebonyi–Abakaliki, Plateau–Jos, Ogun–Abeokuta). The original school-source questions are not changed. This supplement is new teaching content, not a claim that state capitals were in the Week 1 scheme.

lessons.subject: Geography
lessons.title: The Solar System and the Universe
objectives: Define the solar system, universe, galaxy, satellite and orbit.
Name the eight planets in order from the Sun and distinguish rotation from revolution.
Describe important characteristics of the eight planets and explain Pluto's dwarf-planet classification.
Answer the Week Two source evaluation and theory questions using current, accurate astronomy.
lessons.body:
THE SOLAR SYSTEM AND THE UNIVERSE

Learning focus
By the end of this lesson, you should be able to define the solar system, universe, galaxy, satellite and orbit; name the eight planets in order from the Sun; distinguish rotation from revolution; describe important features of each planet; and explain why Pluto is classified as a dwarf planet.

1. The solar system
The solar system is the Sun and all the objects held by its gravity that travel around it. These include eight planets, their natural satellites (moons), dwarf planets, asteroids, comets and smaller bodies. The Sun is a star. It supplies most of the light and heat used by the planets. The planets do not produce their own visible light like the Sun; they reflect sunlight.

A planet follows a path called an orbit around the Sun. Planetary orbits are elliptical, which means they are slightly oval rather than perfect circles. Revolution is the movement of a planet around the Sun. Rotation is the spinning of a body on its axis. Earth takes about 365¼ days to complete one revolution and about 24 hours to complete one rotation.

2. The eight planets in order
Starting nearest to the Sun, the eight planets are Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune. A memory aid is: My Very Educated Mother Just Served Us Noodles.

Mercury is the smallest planet and the nearest to the Sun. It has no moon. Its surface becomes very hot in daylight and extremely cold at night because it has almost no atmosphere to retain heat. It is not the hottest planet.

Venus is the second planet from the Sun. It is similar to Earth in size and is sometimes called Earth's twin, but its surface conditions are very different. Its thick atmosphere traps heat, making Venus the hottest planet. Venus has no moon and rotates in the opposite direction to most planets.

Earth is the third planet from the Sun. It has one natural satellite, the Moon. Earth is the only world on which life is known to exist. Liquid water and a life-supporting atmosphere are among the conditions that make life possible. Earth has gravity, but gravity is not unique to Earth; all objects with mass exert gravity.

Mars is the fourth planet. It is often called the Red Planet because iron-rich dust gives much of its surface a reddish appearance. Mars has two small moons, Phobos and Deimos.

Jupiter is the fifth planet and the largest planet in the solar system. It is a gas giant with bands of clouds and a very large storm known as the Great Red Spot. It has many moons.

Saturn is the sixth planet. It is a gas giant best known for its broad and bright ring system. The rings are made mainly of pieces of ice and rocky material; they are not simply three solid rings. Saturn also has many moons.

Uranus is the seventh planet. It is an ice giant with a blue-green appearance. Its axis is tilted so far that it appears to rotate on its side. Its rotation is retrograde, meaning opposite to the direction used by most planets.

Neptune is the eighth and most distant of the eight planets from the Sun. It is an ice giant with a very cold atmosphere and extremely fast winds.

3. Pluto and the dwarf planets
The original school note calls Pluto the ninth planet and includes it in a table of nine planets. This is an outdated classification. In 2006, the International Astronomical Union defined a planet as an object that orbits the Sun, is nearly round because of its own gravity, and has cleared the neighbourhood around its orbit. Pluto meets the first two conditions but has not cleared its orbital neighbourhood. It is therefore classified as a dwarf planet, not one of the eight planets. Pluto remains an important member of the solar system.

4. The universe, galaxies and satellites
The universe includes all space, time, matter and energy. It contains an enormous number of galaxies. A galaxy is a huge system of stars, gas, dust and other matter held together by gravity. Our solar system is in the Milky Way galaxy. The Milky Way contains far more than a few dozen stars; it contains hundreds of billions of stars.

A satellite is an object that moves around a larger body. A natural satellite is not made by people. The Moon is Earth's natural satellite. Artificial satellites are built by people and placed in orbit for purposes such as communication, weather observation and navigation.

5. Important corrections to the older source table and descriptions
Use the eight-planet classification, not a list of nine planets. Pluto is a dwarf planet. Mercury is nearest to the Sun but Venus is the hottest planet. Earth is the only planet currently known to support life, but oxygen and gravity are not exclusive to Earth. Saturn has a complex ring system, not only three rings. Uranus is not accurately described as the only planet rotating clockwise; its axis is extremely tilted and its rotation is retrograde. Counts of moons change as new moons are confirmed, so learn the stable facts above rather than memorising the old source table's satellite counts. Distances and orbital periods in the source table are approximate and should not be treated as precise current measurements.

6. Answers to the source evaluation and theory questions
A solar system is a star and the objects that orbit it under gravity. Our solar system includes the Sun, eight planets, moons, dwarf planets, asteroids and comets.
A galaxy is a vast collection of stars, gas, dust and other matter held together by gravity. A satellite moves around a planet or another larger body. An orbit is the path followed by an object as it moves around another body.
The universe is the totality of space, time, matter and energy; it contains galaxies, stars, planets and many other objects.
One characteristic of each planet: Mercury is the smallest and nearest to the Sun; Venus is the hottest; Earth has liquid water and is the only known world with life; Mars is reddish and has two moons; Jupiter is the largest; Saturn has prominent rings; Uranus rotates on a strongly tilted axis; Neptune is the most distant of the eight planets.
The first four planets are Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars. Mercury is small and nearest the Sun; Venus is second and hottest; Earth is the third planet and has one Moon; Mars is the fourth and appears red.
The last of the eight planets is Neptune. It is farthest from the Sun among the eight planets and has a cold atmosphere with very fast winds.
Earth's natural satellite is the Moon.

7. Source question review
The source asks which statement is not true: that all planets 'rotate around' the Sun or that they 'revolve around' the Sun. The wording is ambiguous because 'rotate around' is sometimes used informally to mean orbit, while rotation properly means spinning on an axis. Do not score this item until it is rewritten as: 'Which statement correctly describes a planet's revolution? Answer: It moves around the Sun along an orbit.'
The source asks which two planets lie between the Sun and Earth. The answer is Mercury and Venus.
The source asks which planet has the largest orbit and offers Pluto. Under the current classification, Pluto is a dwarf planet; among the eight planets, Neptune is farthest from the Sun. Rewrite the item to ask 'Which of the eight planets is farthest from the Sun?' Answer: Neptune.
The source asks which planet has no satellite and gives Venus, Uranus and Neptune as options. Venus is the correct option among those choices; Mercury also has no moon.
The source calls Venus Earth's twin because of similarities in size, mass and density. Venus is similar in size to Earth, but its environment is extremely different.

PRACTICE
1. Define solar system, galaxy, satellite and orbit.
2. List the eight planets in order from the Sun.
3. Explain the difference between rotation and revolution.
4. State one important characteristic of each of the eight planets.
5. Explain why Pluto is a dwarf planet rather than one of the eight planets.
6. Why is Venus hotter than Mercury even though Mercury is nearer to the Sun?
7. Name Earth's natural satellite and state two uses of artificial satellites.

ANSWER GUIDE
1. Solar system: the Sun and objects that orbit it under gravity. Galaxy: a huge system of stars, gas, dust and other matter held by gravity. Satellite: an object that moves around a larger body. Orbit: the path followed by an orbiting object. Award 1 mark for each correct definition (4 marks).
2. Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune (4 marks; 0.5 mark each in order).
3. Rotation is spinning on an axis; revolution is movement around another body, in this lesson a planet moving around the Sun. Award 2 marks for each clear definition (4 marks).
4. Award 1 mark for one accurate characteristic for each named planet, up to 8 marks. Accept the characteristics in section 2.
5. Pluto orbits the Sun and is nearly round, but it has not cleared its orbital neighbourhood; the IAU therefore classifies it as a dwarf planet (3 marks).
6. Venus has a dense atmosphere that traps heat through a strong greenhouse effect; Mercury has almost no atmosphere to retain heat (3 marks).
7. The Moon (1 mark). Artificial satellites are used for communication, weather monitoring, navigation, Earth observation or scientific research; award 1 mark for each of any two (3 marks).

Total: 29 marks. Teachers may adapt the total while preserving the stated item-level marking.

SOURCES AND PROVENANCE
This is an original SS1 teaching supplement based on the school's First Term Geography Week Two topic and assessment prompts. It preserves the source's topic sequence but corrects outdated or inaccurate astronomy claims rather than reproducing them as current facts. The original source document remains unchanged.
The International Astronomical Union's 2006 Resolution 5A and Resolution 6A classify the eight planets and Pluto as a dwarf planet: https://www.iau.org/IAU/Iau/News/PR2006/iau-2006-general-assembly-resolution-votes.aspx
NASA Solar System Facts confirms the solar system has eight planets and describes the Milky Way: https://science.nasa.gov/solar-system/solar-system-facts/
NASA Mercury Facts confirms Mercury is nearest to the Sun and not the hottest planet: https://science.nasa.gov/mercury/facts/
NASA Venus Facts identifies Venus as the hottest planet: https://science.nasa.gov/venus/venus-facts/
The school's reading pointer 'Essential Geography, O.A. Iwena, pages 5-7' is recorded in the source, but that book was not supplied for inspection; the page range and its contents are not independently verified by this supplement.

lessons.subject: Geography
lessons.title: Earth as a Planet: Shape, Size and Movements
objectives: Describe Earth's approximate shape and size using accurate measurements.
Explain evidence that Earth is approximately spherical.
Define rotation and revolution and describe their effects.
Explain how Earth's axial tilt and revolution produce seasons, changing daylight and eclipses.
lessons.body:
EARTH AS A PLANET: SHAPE, SIZE AND MOVEMENTS

Learning focus
By the end of this lesson, you should be able to describe Earth's shape and size; explain evidence that Earth is not flat; distinguish rotation from revolution; describe the effects of each movement; explain the role of axial tilt in seasons; and define dawn and twilight.

1. The shape of the Earth
Earth is approximately spherical, but it is not a perfect sphere. It is slightly flattened at the North and South Poles and bulges around the Equator. This approximate mathematical shape is called an oblate spheroid. The word geoid is also used in geography, but it has a more precise meaning: it describes an irregular surface related to Earth's gravity field that closely matches mean sea level extended beneath the continents. For simple classroom description, say that Earth is nearly spherical and slightly flattened at the poles; do not treat the geoid as a perfect ball.

2. The size of the Earth
Earth is the fifth-largest planet in the solar system. Its equatorial diameter is about 12,756 kilometres. Its polar diameter is about 12,714 kilometres. The equatorial circumference is about 40,075 kilometres. These values are approximate and may differ slightly between reference sources because of the way measurements are defined. The total surface area is about 510 million square kilometres. Earth is slightly wider across the Equator than from pole to pole because it rotates.

3. Evidence that the Earth is approximately spherical
(a) Photographs and measurements from space: satellites and spacecraft provide images and precise measurements of Earth's curved shape.
(b) Lunar eclipses: during a lunar eclipse, Earth passes between the Sun and Moon and its shadow falls on the Moon. The curved edge of the shadow is evidence of Earth's round shape.
(c) Ships at the horizon: when a ship moves away, its hull disappears before its mast; when it approaches, the mast may become visible before the lower part of the ship. This is consistent with a curved surface, although visibility, waves and atmospheric conditions also affect what an observer sees.
(d) Circumnavigation: people and ships can travel around the world and return to their starting region without meeting an edge. The expedition led by Ferdinand Magellan began the first circumnavigation in 1519. Magellan died before it was completed; Juan Sebastián Elcano led the surviving expedition back to Spain in 1522. It is therefore inaccurate to say that Magellan personally completed the voyage.
(e) Different stars and horizons: observers at different latitudes see different parts of the sky and different apparent altitudes of stars. The horizon also changes with the observer's position and height.
(f) Geodetic surveys: measurements using satellites, GPS and surveying instruments establish Earth's curved, slightly flattened shape.

4. Rotation of the Earth
Rotation is the spinning of Earth on its imaginary axis, an imaginary line running through the North and South Poles. Earth rotates from west to east. One rotation takes approximately 24 hours when measured from one noon to the next; relative to distant stars it takes about 23 hours 56 minutes. For SS1 calculations, use 24 hours unless a question states otherwise.

Earth turns through 360 degrees in about 24 hours. Therefore:
- 360° ÷ 24 = 15° per hour.
- 15° ÷ 60 = 0.25° per minute.
- 1° corresponds to about 4 minutes of time.
Places east of another place generally experience local noon earlier because Earth rotates eastward; places to the west experience it later.

Main effects of rotation
1. Day and night: the half of Earth facing the Sun has daylight; the half turned away has night. Rotation carries places into and out of sunlight.
2. Apparent daily movement of the Sun and stars: the sky appears to move from east to west because Earth rotates from west to east.
3. Differences in local time: places at different longitudes face the Sun at different times. The approximate relationship is 15 degrees of longitude per hour, or 1 degree per four minutes.
4. Deflection of moving air and water: Earth's rotation contributes to the Coriolis effect. Moving air and water are deflected to the right in the Northern Hemisphere and to the left in the Southern Hemisphere. The effect influences large-scale winds and ocean currents; it does not mean every small moving object visibly curves.
5. The daily cycle of tides: the Moon's gravity, and to a lesser extent the Sun's gravity, produce tidal forces. Earth's rotation carries coastal locations through changing tidal conditions. Rotation alone does not create the tides.

5. Revolution of the Earth
Revolution is the movement of one body around another along an orbit. Earth revolves around the Sun and completes one orbit in about 365.2422 days, commonly written as approximately 365¼ days. The Moon revolves around Earth. Earth and the Moon travel together around the Sun.

A calendar year normally has 365 days. The extra fraction of a day is managed by leap years. In the Gregorian calendar, a year divisible by four is usually a leap year; a century year is not a leap year unless it is also divisible by 400. A leap year has 366 days.

Main effects of revolution together with Earth's axial tilt
1. A year: the time Earth takes to complete one orbit around the Sun defines the length of the year.
2. Seasons: Earth's axis is tilted by about 23.4 degrees relative to the plane of its orbit. As Earth revolves around the Sun, each hemisphere is tilted towards or away from the Sun at different times. This change in the angle and duration of sunlight produces the seasons. The Northern and Southern Hemispheres have opposite seasons. Seasons are not caused by Earth simply being nearer to or farther from the Sun.
3. Changes in the Sun's midday height: the Sun appears higher or lower in the sky at midday at different times of the year because of Earth's axial tilt and orbital position.
4. Changes in day and night length: outside the Equator, the length of daylight changes through the year. The amount of change depends on latitude; near the poles, periods of continuous daylight or darkness can occur.
5. Seasonal temperature changes: the angle and duration of incoming sunlight affect heating. Local weather, clouds, oceans and land also influence temperature, so seasons are not identical everywhere.

6. Equinoxes, solstices, dawn and twilight
An equinox occurs when the Sun is positioned over the Equator and day and night are approximately equal in length across much of Earth. A solstice occurs when the Sun reaches its greatest apparent northward or southward position; these dates mark the longest and shortest daylight periods in each hemisphere.
Dawn is the period of increasing light before sunrise. Twilight is the period when sunlight still illuminates the sky after sunset or before sunrise, even though the Sun is below the horizon. Dawn and twilight are not the same as sunrise and sunset.

7. Eclipses
A solar eclipse occurs when the Moon passes between Earth and the Sun and blocks all or part of the Sun from view for observers in the Moon's shadow. A lunar eclipse occurs when Earth is between the Sun and Moon and Earth's shadow falls on the Moon. A solar eclipse occurs at new Moon and a lunar eclipse at full Moon, but they do not happen every month because the Moon's orbit is tilted relative to Earth's orbit around the Sun.

8. Answers to the source evaluation and theory questions
Earth's shape: approximately spherical, more precisely an oblate spheroid; geoid is the gravity-related reference surface close to mean sea level.
Earth's size: equatorial diameter about 12,756 km; polar diameter about 12,714 km; equatorial circumference about 40,075 km; surface area about 510 million km². Earth is the fifth-largest planet.
Four proofs of Earth's sphericity: images and measurements from space; Earth's curved shadow during lunar eclipses; ships disappearing hull-first over the horizon; and circumnavigation. Other acceptable evidence includes geodetic surveys and changes in the visible sky with latitude.
The Magellan expedition began the first circumnavigation in 1519; Magellan died during the voyage. Elcano led the surviving expedition that returned to Spain in 1522.
Rotation means spinning on an axis. Its effects include day and night, apparent daily movement of celestial objects, local-time differences and the Coriolis effect. Tides are caused by the gravitational pull of the Moon and Sun, while Earth's rotation helps create the daily pattern experienced at coasts.
Revolution means movement around another body. Earth takes about 365¼ days to orbit the Sun. Together with axial tilt, revolution produces the yearly pattern of seasons and changes in day length and the Sun's midday height.
The Sun appears to rise in the east and set in the west. This is an apparent motion caused mainly by Earth's west-to-east rotation.

PRACTICE
1. Describe Earth's shape. Explain the difference between an oblate spheroid and the geoid.
2. State four measurements or facts that describe Earth's size.
3. Give five pieces of evidence that Earth is approximately spherical.
4. Define rotation and state four effects of Earth's rotation.
5. Define revolution and explain why Earth has seasons.
6. Distinguish an equinox from a solstice.
7. Explain the difference between a solar eclipse and a lunar eclipse.
8. Correct this statement: 'Magellan was the first person to sail around the world and personally completed the journey.'
9. A place is 30° east of Greenwich. Using 15° per hour, calculate its approximate local-time difference from Greenwich.

ANSWER GUIDE
1. Earth is nearly spherical and slightly flattened at the poles; an oblate spheroid is the smooth mathematical approximation, while the geoid is an irregular gravity-related surface close to mean sea level. Award 2 marks for shape and 2 for the distinction (4 marks).
2. Any four: equatorial diameter about 12,756 km; polar diameter about 12,714 km; equatorial circumference about 40,075 km; surface area about 510 million km²; fifth-largest planet. Award 1 mark each (4 marks).
3. Any five valid proofs from section 3, each briefly explained (5 marks).
4. Rotation is spinning on an axis (2 marks). Award 1 mark each for four valid effects (4 marks). Total 6 marks.
5. Revolution is Earth's movement around the Sun along an orbit (2 marks). Seasons occur because Earth's axis is tilted about 23.4°; as Earth revolves, each hemisphere receives different angles and durations of sunlight (3 marks). Total 5 marks.
6. Equinox: Sun over the Equator and day/night approximately equal. Solstice: Sun reaches its greatest apparent north/south position, producing longest or shortest daylight. Award 2 marks each (4 marks).
7. Solar: Moon between Earth and Sun. Lunar: Earth between Sun and Moon, Earth's shadow falling on the Moon. Award 2 marks each (4 marks).
8. Magellan led the expedition that began in 1519 but died before it finished; Elcano led the surviving crew back to Spain in 1522. Award 2 marks for Magellan's role and 2 for Elcano's completion (4 marks).
9. 30° ÷ 15° per hour = 2 hours. A place east is ahead, so the local time is approximately 2 hours ahead of Greenwich (2 marks: calculation 1, direction 1).

Total: 38 marks. The marking breakdown is explicit so a teacher can adjust the total without guessing how marks are awarded.

lessons.subject: Geography
lessons.title: Latitude, Longitude, Great Circles and Small Circles
objectives: Define latitude and longitude and identify their reference lines.
Identify the major parallels and explain the range of latitude and longitude.
Compare parallels and meridians and explain how coordinates locate places.
Distinguish great circles from small circles and explain the shortest-route property.
lessons.body:
LATITUDE, LONGITUDE, GREAT CIRCLES AND SMALL CIRCLES

Learning focus
By the end of this lesson, you should be able to define latitude and longitude; identify the major parallels and meridians; use latitude and longitude together to locate places; compare parallels and meridians; and distinguish great circles from small circles.

1. Latitude
Latitude is the angular distance of a place north or south of the Equator, measured at the centre of Earth. The Equator is 0° latitude. Latitude values run from 0° to 90° north (N) and from 0° to 90° south (S). A latitude is written with its degree value and hemisphere, for example 6°N or 12°S.

Lines of latitude are also called parallels because they run east-west and remain parallel to one another. They are circles around Earth. The Equator is the largest parallel and is a great circle. Other parallels become smaller towards the poles; at 90°N and 90°S they meet at the North and South Poles, which are points rather than full circles.

Important parallels
- Equator: 0°.
- Tropic of Cancer: about 23½°N.
- Tropic of Capricorn: about 23½°S.
- Arctic Circle: about 66½°N.
- Antarctic Circle: about 66½°S.
- North Pole: 90°N.
- South Pole: 90°S.

Latitude is useful for identifying the north-south position of a place, locating places on maps and globes, and estimating north-south distances. A degree of latitude is approximately 111 kilometres, although the exact distance varies slightly; detailed distance calculations are studied separately.

2. Longitude
Longitude is the angular distance of a place east or west of the Prime Meridian, measured around Earth's axis. The Prime Meridian is 0° longitude and passes through Greenwich, England. Longitude values extend from 0° to 180° east (E) and from 0° to 180° west (W). The 180° meridian is opposite the Prime Meridian and is close to the International Date Line, although the date line bends to avoid dividing countries and island groups.

Lines of longitude are called meridians. They run from the North Pole to the South Pole and meet at both poles. Each meridian is a semicircle; a meridian together with the opposite meridian forms a complete great circle. All meridians have the same length on a globe. Longitude is essential for locating places and calculating differences in local time. Latitude alone does not determine local time.

3. Latitude and longitude as a location grid
A location is identified by giving its latitude and longitude together. Latitude is written first, followed by longitude. For example, a coordinate is written in the form 6°N, 3°E. The letters N/S identify the hemisphere north or south of the Equator; E/W identify the hemisphere east or west of Greenwich. Coordinates may also be written in degrees, minutes and seconds or in decimal degrees.

4. Similarities and differences
Similarities
- Both are imaginary reference lines used on globes and maps.
- Both are measured as angles in degrees.
- Both help identify the location of a place when used together.
- Both form part of the geographic grid (graticule).

Differences
- Latitude measures north or south of the Equator; longitude measures east or west of the Prime Meridian.
- Parallels run east-west; meridians run north-south from pole to pole.
- Parallels do not meet one another; meridians converge at the poles.
- The Equator is the only latitude circle that is a great circle. A pair of opposite meridians forms a great circle.
- Parallels become smaller towards the poles; all meridians have the same semicircular length.
- Latitude ranges from 0° to 90°N or 90°S; longitude ranges from 0° to 180°E or 180°W.
- Latitude is useful for north-south position and distance; longitude is used to establish east-west position and local-time differences.

5. Great circles
A great circle is a circle on a sphere whose plane passes through the centre of the sphere. It divides the sphere into two equal hemispheres and is the largest possible circle on the sphere. The Equator is a great circle. A complete great circle can also be formed by pairing two opposite meridians, such as 0° and 180°.

The shortest surface route between two points on a sphere follows an arc of a great circle. This is why great-circle routes are important in long-distance air and sea navigation. On a flat map, a great-circle route may appear curved because the curved Earth has been projected onto a flat surface.

6. Small circles
A small circle is a circle on a sphere whose plane does not pass through the sphere's centre. It does not divide the sphere into two equal hemispheres. Most lines of latitude are small circles, including the Tropics of Cancer and Capricorn and the Arctic and Antarctic Circles. The Equator is the exception because it is a great circle. At the poles, the 90° parallels reduce to points.

7. Answers to the source evaluation and theory questions
Latitude is the angular distance north or south of the Equator, measured at Earth's centre. The major parallels are the Equator (0°), Tropic of Cancer (23½°N), Tropic of Capricorn (23½°S), Arctic Circle (66½°N), Antarctic Circle (66½°S), North Pole (90°N) and South Pole (90°S).
Longitude is the angular distance east or west of the Greenwich Prime Meridian. The major meridians used as references include 0° (Prime Meridian), 180° (opposite meridian), and any stated east or west meridian such as 45°E or 90°W.
Two similarities: both are imaginary angular reference lines; both are measured in degrees and used together to locate places. Four differences: latitude runs east-west while longitude runs north-south; latitude is measured from the Equator while longitude is measured from Greenwich; parallels do not meet while meridians meet at the poles; latitude extends to 90°N/S while longitude extends to 180°E/W.
A great circle is a circle whose plane passes through Earth's centre and divides Earth into two equal hemispheres. A small circle does not pass through Earth's centre and does not divide Earth into equal hemispheres.

PRACTICE
1. Define latitude and longitude.
2. List the five major parallels and give their approximate positions.
3. Explain how latitude and longitude are used together to locate a place.
4. State four similarities and four differences between parallels and meridians.
5. Define a great circle and a small circle. Give two examples of each.
6. Explain why a pair of opposite meridians forms a great circle but one meridian alone does not.
7. Choose the correct answer: Which coordinate tells how far a place is east or west of Greenwich? (a) latitude (b) longitude (c) altitude.
8. Choose the correct answer: Which statement about latitude is correct? (a) It ranges from 0° to 180° north. (b) It measures east and west of Greenwich. (c) It ranges from 0° to 90° north or south.

ANSWER GUIDE
1. Latitude: angular distance north or south of the Equator. Longitude: angular distance east or west of the Prime Meridian. Award 2 marks each (4 marks).
2. Equator 0°; Tropic of Cancer 23½°N; Tropic of Capricorn 23½°S; Arctic Circle 66½°N; Antarctic Circle 66½°S. Award 1 mark each (5 marks).
3. Give latitude first to show north/south position, then longitude to show east/west position. The two coordinates identify a point on the geographic grid. Award 3 marks (3 marks).
4. Award 1 mark for each of four correct similarities (4 marks) and 1 mark for each of four correct differences (4 marks). Accept the points in section 4. Total 8 marks.
5. Great circle: circle whose plane passes through the centre; examples include the Equator and a complete pair of opposite meridians. Small circle: circle whose plane does not pass through the centre; examples include the Tropic of Cancer and Tropic of Capricorn. Award 2 marks for each definition and 1 mark for each of two valid examples (6 marks).
6. One meridian is only a semicircle from pole to pole. Its opposite meridian completes the circle through Earth's centre, dividing Earth into two hemispheres. Award 3 marks.
7. (b) longitude (1 mark).
8. (c) it ranges from 0° to 90° north or south (1 mark).

Total: 31 marks.

SOURCE QUESTION REVIEW
The source says latitude “measures up to 180°” and then gives 90°N–90°S. The correct range is 0° to 90° in either hemisphere; do not describe it as a single 180° latitude value. The source's similarity option that both latitude and longitude are used to calculate local time is not correct: longitude is used for local-time differences, while latitude is not. The source's great-circle multiple-choice wording mixes a definition with a property; the supplement gives the exact geometric definition and separately explains the shortest-route property. The source's examples of opposite meridians must be pairs 180° apart; arbitrary pairs such as 30°W and 15°W do not form a great circle.

U.S. Geological Survey, The Universal Transverse Mercator (UTM) grid: https://www.usgs.gov/publications/universal-transverse-mercator-utm-grid-1 (parallels and meridians as geographic reference lines).

lessons.subject: Geography
lessons.title: Calculating Distance and Local Time
objectives: Calculate approximate north-south distance using differences in latitude.
Calculate local solar time using longitude differences.
Apply east-ahead and west-behind rules and handle date changes.
Distinguish local solar time from official standard time.
lessons.body:
CALCULATING DISTANCE AND LOCAL TIME

Learning focus
By the end of this lesson, you should be able to calculate approximate north-south distance from a difference in latitude; calculate local-time differences from a difference in longitude; decide whether to add or subtract time; and identify when a date change is required.

1. Distance from latitude
One degree of latitude is approximately 111 kilometres along a meridian. This is a useful school-level estimate. It is most directly used to calculate north-south distance between two places on the same or nearby meridian. It does not by itself give the full surface distance between places that are far apart east-west.

Steps
1. Write the latitude of each place, including N or S.
2. If both places are in the same hemisphere, subtract the smaller latitude value from the larger.
3. If the places are in opposite hemispheres, add the two latitude values.
4. Multiply the latitude difference by 111 km.

Worked example 1
Find the approximate north-south distance between a place at 30°S and a place at 40°N.
The places are in opposite hemispheres, so latitude difference = 30° + 40° = 70°.
Distance = 70 × 111 km = 7,770 km.
Answer: approximately 7,770 km.

Worked example 2
Find the approximate distance from the Equator to a place at 14°N.
Latitude difference = 14°.
Distance = 14 × 111 km = 1,554 km.
Answer: approximately 1,554 km north of the Equator.

Worked example 3
Find the approximate north-south distance between 20°S and 51°N.
The places are in opposite hemispheres, so latitude difference = 20° + 51° = 71°.
Distance = 71 × 111 km = 7,881 km.

2. Calculating local time from longitude
Earth rotates through 360° in approximately 24 hours. Therefore:
- 360° ÷ 24 = 15° per hour.
- 1° of longitude corresponds to 4 minutes of local-time difference.
- 15° east or west of a reference meridian corresponds to about one hour.

Steps
1. Write the longitude of each place, including E or W.
2. Find the longitude difference. Add the values when the places are on opposite sides of Greenwich; subtract when they are on the same side.
3. Convert the difference to time: divide degrees by 15 to get hours, or multiply degrees by 4 to get minutes.
4. Decide the direction: a place east is ahead in local solar time; a place west is behind.
5. Add or subtract the time from the reference time. If the calculation passes midnight, change the day. For longitudes crossing the 180° meridian, state the direction and date carefully; the International Date Line is a practical date boundary and does not follow a perfectly straight line.

Worked example 4
At Town A (75°W) the local time is 5:00 p.m. on Friday. Find the local time at Town B (120°E).
Longitude difference = 75° + 120° = 195°.
Time difference = 195° ÷ 15° per hour = 13 hours.
Town B is east of Town A, so its local solar time is ahead.
5:00 p.m. Friday + 13 hours = 6:00 a.m. Saturday.
Answer: approximately 6:00 a.m. on Saturday.

Worked example 5: time from Greenwich
If it is 2:00 p.m. at Greenwich (0°):
- At 45°E: 45 ÷ 15 = 3 hours ahead, so 5:00 p.m. the same day.
- At 75°W: 75 ÷ 15 = 5 hours behind, so 9:00 a.m. the same day.
- At 15°E: 15 ÷ 15 = 1 hour ahead, so 3:00 p.m. the same day.

3. Important reminders
- East is ahead; west is behind.
- Same hemisphere latitudes: subtract. Opposite hemisphere latitudes: add.
- A degree of latitude is about 111 km. Use this for north-south distance, not as a complete east-west or diagonal route calculation.
- For longitude, 15° = 1 hour and 1° = 4 minutes.
- Local solar time is not always identical to a country's official clock time. Countries use standard time zones for administration; some countries use half-hour or quarter-hour offsets and some use daylight-saving time.
- The source's old question about a planet having twelve satellites is not suitable for a current assessment because confirmed moon counts change. Do not memorise the old count or use it as a keyed question.

4. Answers to the source evaluation and general evaluation questions
Distance from 20°S to 51°N: 20° + 51° = 71°; 71 × 111 km = 7,881 km.
Distance from the Equator to Lagos at 14°N: 14 × 111 km = approximately 1,554 km.
To calculate local time, find the longitude difference, convert at 15° per hour (or 4 minutes per degree), then add for east or subtract for west. Check whether the date changes.
If Greenwich time is 2:00 p.m., Ethiopia at 45°E is 5:00 p.m.; Los Angeles at 75°W is 9:00 a.m.; Nigeria at 15°E is 3:00 p.m. under the exercise's local-solar-time assumption.

5. Answers to the source weekend assignment
1. At 75°W, local time is five hours behind Greenwich. 11:00 a.m. − 5 hours = 6:00 a.m.; option (a).
2. Lines of longitude do not run east-west; they run north-south and converge at the poles; option (b).
3. 66½°S is the Antarctic Circle; option (a).
4. 14° × 111 km = 1,554 km, approximately 1,555 km; option (b).
5. The old question asks which planet has twelve satellites. It has no reliable current answer from its options because confirmed moon counts have changed substantially. Do not score or reuse this question; replace it with a stable question such as: “Which of Mercury, Jupiter and Saturn has no natural satellite?” Answer: Mercury.

PRACTICE
1. Calculate the approximate north-south distance between 18°N and 32°N.
2. Calculate the approximate north-south distance between 12°S and 25°N.
3. Calculate the approximate distance from the Equator to a place at 9°S.
4. If it is 10:00 a.m. at Greenwich, what is the local solar time at 30°E?
5. If it is 8:00 p.m. at Greenwich on Monday, what is the local solar time at 45°W?
6. Town A is at 60°W and Town B is at 30°E. If Town A's local time is 7:00 a.m. on Tuesday, calculate Town B's local time and day.
7. Explain why one degree of latitude can be used for an approximate north-south distance but longitude degrees do not represent the same ground distance everywhere.
8. State two reasons why a country's official clock time may differ from its local solar time.

ANSWER GUIDE
1. Same hemisphere: 32° − 18° = 14°. Distance = 14 × 111 = 1,554 km (2 marks: difference 1, multiplication 1).
2. Opposite hemispheres: 12° + 25° = 37°. Distance = 37 × 111 = 4,107 km (2 marks).
3. 9° × 111 = 999 km (2 marks).
4. 30° ÷ 15 = 2 hours ahead. 10:00 a.m. + 2 hours = 12:00 noon (2 marks).
5. 45° ÷ 15 = 3 hours behind. 8:00 p.m. − 3 hours = 5:00 p.m. Monday (2 marks).
6. Longitude difference = 60° + 30° = 90°. Time difference = 90° ÷ 15 = 6 hours. Town B is east, so it is 6 hours ahead: 1:00 p.m. Tuesday (3 marks: difference 1, conversion 1, direction/time 1).
7. Latitude lines are nearly evenly spaced, so a degree of latitude is about 111 km. Meridians converge towards the poles, so the ground distance represented by a degree of longitude becomes smaller at higher latitudes (3 marks).
8. Any two: countries choose a standard time zone for administration; a country may span several longitudes but use one clock time; some countries use half-hour/quarter-hour offsets; daylight-saving time may shift clocks seasonally (2 marks).

Total: 18 marks.

lessons.subject: Geography
lessons.title: The Outer Structure of the Earth
objectives: Identify the lithosphere, hydrosphere, atmosphere and biosphere as interacting outer spheres.
Describe the characteristics and importance of each sphere.
State the main gases in dry air using current approximate percentages.
Explain how the four spheres interact and support life.
lessons.body:
THE OUTER STRUCTURE OF THE EARTH

Learning focus
By the end of this lesson, you should be able to identify the four major Earth systems studied as the outer spheres; describe the lithosphere, hydrosphere, atmosphere and biosphere; explain their importance to people and living things; and state the main gases in dry air.

1. Earth's outer spheres
Geographers describe four closely connected outer spheres of Earth: the lithosphere, hydrosphere, atmosphere and biosphere. They are not four separate concentric layers. They overlap and interact. For example, a tree grows in soil (lithosphere), uses water (hydrosphere), takes in gases from the air (atmosphere) and is part of the biosphere.

2. The lithosphere
The lithosphere is Earth's rigid outer shell. It includes the crust and the uppermost rigid part of the mantle. It consists of solid rocks and minerals and forms the ground on which people build settlements, roads and farms. About 29% of Earth's surface is land; the lithosphere also extends beneath the oceans, so it is not correct to say that the lithosphere itself occupies only 30% of Earth's surface.

Importance of the lithosphere
- It provides land and a foundation for homes, schools, roads and other settlements.
- It supplies mineral resources and rocks used in industry and construction.
- Its soils support crop production and vegetation.
- It provides land for transport routes, recreation and many human activities.
- It contains materials and energy resources that people extract and use responsibly.

3. The hydrosphere
The hydrosphere is all the water on, under and above Earth's surface. It includes oceans, seas, rivers, streams, lakes, groundwater, glaciers and ice, and water vapour in the atmosphere. About 71% of Earth's surface is covered by water. Most of Earth's water is salty ocean water; only a small fraction is freshwater that people can readily use.

Importance of the hydrosphere
- It provides water for drinking, cooking, washing and sanitation.
- It supplies water for agriculture and many industries.
- Rivers, lakes, seas and oceans provide routes for transport and trade.
- It supports fish and other aquatic organisms used as food.
- It supports fishing, tourism and other employment.
- Flowing water can be used to generate hydroelectric power.
- It helps regulate climate and is essential to the water cycle and ecosystems.

4. The atmosphere
The atmosphere is the layer of gases surrounding Earth. In dry air near the surface, nitrogen makes up about 78.08%, oxygen about 20.95%, argon about 0.93% and carbon dioxide about 0.04%; other gases occur in smaller amounts. Water vapour is variable and is not included in the dry-air percentages. The exact amounts of some trace gases, especially carbon dioxide, change over time.

Importance of the atmosphere
- It supplies oxygen needed by humans and many other organisms for respiration.
- It contains carbon dioxide used by plants during photosynthesis.
- It provides nitrogen, but most plants cannot use nitrogen gas directly; nitrogen-fixing organisms and other processes convert it into forms plants can absorb.
- It supports weather and the water cycle, including clouds and rainfall.
- It helps regulate Earth's temperature and protects life from much harmful solar radiation; the ozone layer absorbs much of the Sun's harmful ultraviolet radiation.
- It provides the air through which birds, aircraft and airborne seeds move.

5. The biosphere
The biosphere is the part of Earth where life exists. It includes plants, animals, fungi and microorganisms and the parts of land, water and air that support them. It is not a separate solid layer; it overlaps with the lithosphere, hydrosphere and atmosphere.

Importance of the biosphere
- Plants and animals provide food for people and other organisms.
- Living things provide raw materials such as timber, fibres and some medicines.
- Ecosystems support jobs and livelihoods in farming, fishing, forestry and tourism.
- Plants absorb carbon dioxide and release oxygen during photosynthesis; organisms and ecosystems help cycle nutrients and maintain environmental balance.
- Biodiversity supports healthy, resilient ecosystems.

6. How the four spheres interact
A farmer grows crops in soil (lithosphere), supplies water to them (hydrosphere), relies on air and sunlight (atmosphere) and works with living plants, insects and soil organisms (biosphere). Pollution in one sphere can affect the others: chemicals washed from land can enter rivers; smoke released into the air can affect people, plants and water; loss of vegetation can increase soil erosion.

7. Answers to the source evaluation and weekend questions
The water-covered part of Earth's surface is associated with the hydrosphere. Four benefits include domestic water, industrial and agricultural water, transport, food, employment, tourism and hydroelectric power.
The four outer spheres are lithosphere, hydrosphere, atmosphere and biosphere.
Three benefits of the atmosphere include oxygen for respiration, carbon dioxide for photosynthesis, weather and rainfall, temperature regulation and protection from harmful radiation.
The main gases in dry air are nitrogen (about 78.08%), oxygen (about 20.95%), argon (about 0.93%) and carbon dioxide (about 0.04%), with other trace gases.
The part of Earth where living things exist is the biosphere. Oxygen is about 21% of dry air. Olivine is a mineral; magnesium and aluminium are chemical elements. Humans live on land at the surface of the lithosphere and are part of the biosphere. The water sphere is the hydrosphere.

PRACTICE
1. Name the four outer spheres of Earth and explain why they are not four separate concentric layers.
2. Define the lithosphere and state three of its importance to people.
3. Define the hydrosphere and state four ways it supports human life and activity.
4. Give the approximate percentages of nitrogen, oxygen, argon and carbon dioxide in dry air.
5. State four importance of the atmosphere.
6. Define the biosphere and explain two ways it interacts with the other spheres.
7. Explain why plants cannot usually use nitrogen gas in the air directly.
8. Correct this statement: “The atmosphere contains 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen and 0.03% carbon dioxide, and plants use nitrogen gas directly to make proteins.”

ANSWER GUIDE
1. Lithosphere, hydrosphere, atmosphere and biosphere (2 marks). They overlap and interact rather than forming four separate concentric shells (2 marks). Total 4.
2. Rigid outer shell comprising the crust and uppermost rigid mantle (2 marks). Any three valid benefits (3 marks). Total 5.
3. All water on, under and above Earth's surface (2 marks). Any four valid benefits (4 marks). Total 6.
4. Nitrogen about 78.08%, oxygen about 20.95%, argon about 0.93%, carbon dioxide about 0.04% (4 marks, 1 each).
5. Any four valid benefits from section 4 (4 marks).
6. The zone where life exists (2 marks); any two clear interactions, such as plants using soil, water and air, or organisms affecting soils and gases (2 marks). Total 4.
7. Nitrogen gas must first be fixed into usable compounds by certain bacteria, lightning or industrial processes; plants absorb nitrogen mainly as nitrate or ammonium compounds (3 marks).
8. Nitrogen and oxygen are approximately correct as rounded values; carbon dioxide is now about 0.04% of dry air rather than 0.03% and varies over time. Plants do not generally use atmospheric nitrogen gas directly; it must be fixed into absorbable compounds. Award 2 marks for the composition correction and 2 for the nitrogen-fixation explanation (4 marks).

Total: 34 marks.

SCOPE NOTE
The source's Week Six theory prompt asks students to draw the internal structure of Earth. The scheme assigns the internal zone to Week Seven, and the next source week is explicitly titled “Internal Structure of the Earth”. This Week Six lesson therefore teaches the outer spheres only; the internal-structure drawing is reserved for Week Seven rather than being introduced prematurely.

SOURCES AND PROVENANCE

lessons.subject: Geography
lessons.title: The Internal Structure of the Earth
objectives: Name the crust, mantle and core in order from Earth's surface to its centre.
Describe the composition, thickness and characteristics of the crust and mantle.
Distinguish the liquid outer core from the solid inner core.
Draw and label a simple cross-section of Earth's internal structure.
lessons.body:
THE INTERNAL STRUCTURE OF THE EARTH

Learning focus
By the end of this lesson, you should be able to name the three main internal layers of Earth; describe the crust, mantle and core; distinguish the liquid outer core from the solid inner core; explain the traditional terms SIAL and SIMA; and draw and label a simple cross-section of Earth's interior.

1. The three main internal layers
Earth's interior is commonly described in three main layers, from the outside towards the centre:
1. Crust — the thin, outermost solid rocky layer.
2. Mantle — the thick layer of hot rock beneath the crust.
3. Core — the central metallic region, made mainly of iron and nickel.

The core has two parts: a liquid outer core and a solid inner core. Therefore, a more detailed diagram shows four subdivisions: crust, mantle, outer core and inner core. The crust and mantle are mainly rocky; the core is metallic.

2. The crust
The crust is Earth's thin, rigid, outermost rocky layer. It is much thinner than the mantle. Continental crust averages about 30 km thick, although it is thicker beneath some mountain ranges. Oceanic crust is thinner and is commonly about 5–10 km thick.

Continental crust is generally less dense and has many granitic rocks. Oceanic crust is generally denser and is commonly basaltic. The older school terms SIAL and SIMA are simplified mnemonics: SIAL refers to silica and aluminium-rich continental crust; SIMA refers to silica- and magnesium-rich material traditionally associated with oceanic crust. These are not two separate modern layers, and the crust is not accurately divided everywhere into a simple upper SIAL layer and lower SIMA layer. Older school notes sometimes give approximate densities of about 2.7 g/cm³ for SIAL and 3.0 g/cm³ for SIMA. Treat these as simplified teaching values, not fixed densities for two universal crustal layers.

Importance and characteristics of the crust
- It is the solid surface on which people live and build.
- It contains soils, rocks and mineral resources.
- It forms the land and ocean-floor surface.
- It is thin and brittle compared with the mantle and core.
- It is broken into tectonic plates together with the rigid uppermost mantle.

3. The mantle
The mantle lies below the crust and extends to a depth of about 2,900 km. It is Earth's thickest major layer. It is made mainly of hot silicate rocks rich in magnesium and iron. Most mantle rock is solid, not a sea of liquid magma. Over very long geological periods, hot mantle rock can deform and flow slowly. This slow movement helps drive plate motion and other geological processes.

The uppermost rigid mantle forms part of the lithosphere with the crust. Beneath it is the weaker, slowly deforming asthenosphere. Olivine is an important mineral in much of the upper mantle. The mantle's density and temperature increase with depth; a single value such as 3.3 g/cm³ is only a simplified school-level approximation for some upper-mantle material, not a constant for the entire mantle.

4. The core
The core is Earth's central metallic region, made mainly of iron and nickel. It is much denser than the rocky mantle and is about 3,480 km in radius.

Outer core: The outer core is a layer of liquid iron-rich metal surrounding the inner core. Movement of this electrically conducting liquid helps generate Earth's magnetic field.

Inner core: The inner core is a solid sphere made mainly of iron and nickel. It remains solid because of the enormous pressure at Earth's centre, even though its temperature is extremely high. The temperature near the inner core is about 5,400°C; the exact value depends on the scientific estimate and reference.

The core is not entirely molten. The outer core is liquid; the inner core is solid. The old term NIFE refers to nickel (Ni) and iron (Fe), but these are chemical elements, not minerals.

5. Simple cross-section of Earth's interior
Use the following text model to plan your drawing. Draw four nested circles or bands and label them from the outside towards the centre:

OUTSIDE → CRUST → MANTLE → LIQUID OUTER CORE → SOLID INNER CORE → CENTRE

Drawing instructions
1. Draw a large circle to represent Earth.
2. Draw a very thin band along the outside and label it CRUST.
3. Draw a much thicker band inside it and label it MANTLE (about 2,900 km thick).
4. Draw a band around the centre and label it OUTER CORE — LIQUID IRON-NICKEL.
5. Draw a small central circle and label it INNER CORE — SOLID IRON-NICKEL.
6. Add a title, a key for the four layers, and the note “not to scale”. The crust is extremely thin compared with the other layers, so it must be exaggerated to remain visible in a classroom drawing.

6. Answers to the source evaluation and theory questions
The three main internal layers are crust, mantle and core. The core is divided into liquid outer core and solid inner core.
The traditional term SIAL combines silica and aluminium; SIMA combines silica and magnesium. These are simplified historical terms, not separate modern geological layers. Older school values are approximately 2.7 g/cm³ for SIAL and 3.0 g/cm³ for SIMA; they are not universal modern layer densities.
The crust is thin, rigid and rocky; continental crust is generally thicker and less dense than oceanic crust. The mantle is about 2,900 km thick and mostly solid rock that can flow slowly over geological time. Olivine is a major mineral in the upper mantle.
The core is mainly iron and nickel. The outer core is liquid and the inner core is solid. The inner core is extremely hot, about 5,400°C, but remains solid under immense pressure.

PRACTICE
1. Name the three main internal layers of Earth in order from the outside to the centre.
2. Explain the difference between continental crust and oceanic crust.
3. What do the terms SIAL and SIMA mean? Why should they be treated as simplified historical terms?
4. State two characteristics of the mantle and give its approximate thickness.
5. Name the main mineral associated with the upper mantle in the source lesson.
6. Describe the composition and physical state of the outer core and inner core.
7. Explain why the inner core remains solid despite its very high temperature.
8. State the traditional approximate density values for SIAL and SIMA.
9. Draw and label a cross-section of Earth's interior, showing the crust, mantle, outer core and inner core.

ANSWER GUIDE
1. Crust, mantle, core (3 marks; 1 each in correct order).
2. Continental crust is generally thicker, less dense and commonly granitic; oceanic crust is thinner, denser and commonly basaltic (4 marks; 2 for each comparison).
3. SIAL = silica and aluminium; SIMA = silica and magnesium (2 marks). They are historical simplified labels and do not describe two separate modern crustal layers everywhere (2 marks). Total 4.
4. The mantle is hot, mainly solid silicate rock that deforms/flows slowly over geological time; it extends about 2,900 km thick (3 marks).
5. Olivine (1 mark).
6. Both are mainly iron-nickel metal; outer core is liquid and inner core is solid (4 marks; composition 2, state 2).
7. The immense pressure at Earth's centre keeps the inner core solid despite its high temperature (2 marks).
8. SIAL about 2.7 g/cm³; SIMA about 3.0 g/cm³. Award 1 mark each (2 marks).
9. Award 1 mark for each correctly labelled layer, 2 marks for correct order and relative proportions, and 1 mark for a title/key and “not to scale” note (7 marks).

Total: 30 marks.

SOURCE QUESTION REVIEW
The source states that the mantle is about 290 km thick; the correct approximate thickness is 2,900 km. It describes the mantle as semi-liquid; most mantle rock is solid but deforms and flows very slowly over geological time. The source describes the whole core as molten and gives a temperature of about 2,000°C; the outer core is liquid, the inner core is solid, and the inner-core temperature is around 5,400°C. The source's SIAL/SIMA and NIFE labels are retained only as historical classroom mnemonics, not as exact modern mineral-layer classifications. The weekend question asking for atmospheric nitrogen percentage is a Week Six carry-over, not an internal-structure objective; its answer is approximately 78% of dry air.

NASA Science, Facts About Earth: https://science.nasa.gov/earth/facts/ (four main layers, core composition and inner-core temperature).
NASA Space Place, Make a Fan with Earth's Layers: https://spaceplace.nasa.gov/earth-fan/en/ (student-level explanation of crust, mantle, outer and inner core).
U.S. Geological Survey, Are the tectonic plates floating on magma?: https://www.usgs.gov/faqs/are-tectonic-plates-floating-magma (mantle behaves as solid rock over short timescales and flows slowly over geological timescales).

lessons.subject: Geography
lessons.title: Rocks of the Earth
objectives: Define rocks and distinguish rocks from minerals.
Describe how igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic rocks form.
Identify common characteristics and examples of the three rock groups.
Explain the rock cycle and the importance of rocks to people.
lessons.body:
ROCKS OF THE EARTH

Learning focus
By the end of this lesson, you should be able to define a rock; identify the three main rock groups; explain how igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic rocks form; describe their characteristics and examples; explain the rock cycle; and state important uses of rocks.

1. What is a rock?
A rock is a naturally occurring solid material made of one or more minerals or mineraloids. Rocks differ in colour, texture, grain size, structure, permeability, strength and the way they occur. A mineral is a naturally occurring substance with a characteristic chemical composition and structure; a rock is usually an aggregate of minerals. For example, granite commonly contains quartz, feldspar and mica.

2. The three main groups of rocks
Rocks are classified by how they form into three main groups:
- Igneous rocks form when molten rock cools and solidifies.
- Sedimentary rocks form when sediments are deposited and become rock, or when minerals precipitate from water or remains of organisms accumulate.
- Metamorphic rocks form when existing rocks are changed by heat, pressure and/or hot fluids without completely melting.

3. Igneous rocks
Igneous rocks form when molten rock cools and solidifies. Molten rock below Earth's surface is called magma. When it reaches the surface, it is called lava.

Intrusive (plutonic) igneous rocks form when magma cools slowly below the surface. Slow cooling gives crystals more time to grow, so these rocks usually have larger visible crystals. Examples include granite, diorite and gabbro.

Extrusive (volcanic) igneous rocks form when lava cools at or near the surface. Cooling is usually faster, so crystals are small or may not be visible. Examples include basalt, andesite and rhyolite.

Common characteristics of igneous rocks
- Many have interlocking crystals and a crystalline texture.
- They are usually not arranged in sedimentary layers.
- They do not normally contain fossils because they form from molten material.
- Many are hard and strong, but their resistance to weathering varies with mineral composition and climate.
- Intrusive rocks generally have larger crystals than extrusive rocks.

4. Sedimentary rocks
Sedimentary rocks form when sediments are produced by weathering and erosion, transported by water, wind or ice, deposited in layers, and gradually compacted and cemented into rock. Some sedimentary rocks form when minerals precipitate from water; others form from the accumulated remains of plants or animals.

Three main groups of sedimentary rocks
A. Mechanically formed (clastic) sedimentary rocks are made from fragments of older rocks. Examples include sandstone, shale, breccia and conglomerate.
B. Organically formed (biogenic) sedimentary rocks form from the remains or activity of living organisms. Chalk and many limestones form largely from shells or skeletal material. Coal forms from accumulated plant remains. Peat and lignite are stages/materials in coal formation. Petroleum is a liquid hydrocarbon fossil fuel formed from buried organic matter; it is not a solid rock.
C. Chemically formed sedimentary rocks form when dissolved minerals precipitate from water, often as water evaporates. Examples include rock salt (halite), gypsum and some dolostone.

Common characteristics of sedimentary rocks
- They often occur in layers called strata.
- They may be coarse-grained or fine-grained, soft or hard.
- Many are made of cemented grains or fragments; others form by chemical or biological processes.
- Fossils are often preserved in sedimentary rocks. The source statement that sedimentary rocks do not contain fossils is incorrect.
- Many sedimentary rocks are more easily weathered or eroded than some igneous and metamorphic rocks, but resistance varies.

5. Metamorphic rocks
Metamorphic rocks form when an existing igneous, sedimentary or older metamorphic rock is changed by heat, pressure and/or hot mineral-rich fluids. The rock changes its minerals, texture or structure but does not completely melt. If it melts and later cools, it forms igneous rock instead.

Examples include slate (often formed from shale), marble (often formed from limestone), quartzite (often formed from sandstone), schist and gneiss. Some metamorphic rocks are foliated, meaning their minerals are arranged in layers or bands; others are non-foliated and have no obvious banding.

6. The rock cycle
Rocks are continually changed by geological processes. Magma cools to form igneous rock. Weathering and erosion break rocks into sediments; deposition, compaction and cementation can form sedimentary rock. Heat and pressure can change igneous or sedimentary rock into metamorphic rock. Any rock may melt and become magma again. Uplift can expose buried rocks at the surface. The rock cycle does not always follow one fixed route; rocks can change through several different pathways.

7. Importance of rocks to people
- Rocks provide building materials such as granite, limestone, marble and slate.
- Crushed rock is used for roads, railways, concrete and construction.
- Rocks contain minerals and ores used in manufacturing and technology.
- Some rocks and associated deposits provide fuels and industrial materials, such as coal, petroleum-bearing formations, limestone and gypsum.
- Weathered rocks help form soil needed for agriculture.
- Rocks preserve fossils and evidence of Earth's past environments.
- Rock landscapes support tourism, recreation and scientific study.

8. Answers to the source evaluation and weekend questions
Two examples of intrusive igneous rocks are granite and diorite (gabbro is also correct). Three characteristics of igneous rocks include crystalline texture, lack of sedimentary layering, usually no fossils, and often hard interlocking crystals.
Two characteristics of sedimentary rocks include layering/strata and the frequent presence of fossils. They form through deposition and lithification (compaction and cementation), chemical precipitation or accumulation of biological remains.
Five uses of rocks include building, road construction, mineral supply, soil formation, industrial materials, fuels, tourism and evidence of Earth's history.
Organically formed sedimentary rocks include coal and many limestones/chalks formed from biological remains. Chemically formed examples include rock salt (halite), gypsum and some dolostone.
Weekend answers: (1) sedimentary rocks; (2) igneous rocks; (3) gneiss; (4) organically formed sedimentary rock; (5) the source item is flawed because both petrol and micro-organisms are not rocks. Replace it with “Which of the following is a sedimentary rock: granite, chalk or gneiss?” Answer: chalk.

PRACTICE
1. Define a rock and explain how a rock differs from a mineral.
2. Name the three main groups of rocks and state how each forms.
3. Distinguish intrusive and extrusive igneous rocks, giving two examples of each.
4. State four characteristics of igneous rocks.
5. Explain how sedimentary rocks form and name the three main groups based on formation.
6. Give three characteristics of sedimentary rocks. Explain why the statement “sedimentary rocks do not contain fossils” is wrong.
7. Explain how metamorphic rocks form and give three examples.
8. Describe the rock cycle using the words magma, cooling, weathering, sediments, compaction, cementation, heat and pressure.
9. State five importance of rocks to people.
10. Identify the rock group: granite, sandstone, marble, basalt, chalk, gneiss and rock salt.

ANSWER GUIDE
1. A rock is a naturally occurring solid made of one or more minerals/mineraloids (2 marks). A mineral has a more definite composition/structure, while a rock is usually an aggregate of minerals (2 marks). Total 4.
2. Igneous: cooling/solidification of magma or lava; sedimentary: deposition and lithification, precipitation or biological accumulation; metamorphic: alteration by heat, pressure and/or fluids without melting (3 marks, 1 each).
3. Intrusive: magma cools slowly below ground, usually large crystals; examples granite and diorite/gabbro. Extrusive: lava cools quickly at/near the surface, usually small crystals; examples basalt and rhyolite/andesite (4 marks).
4. Any four: crystalline/interlocking crystals; usually not layered; normally no fossils; often hard/strong; intrusive forms have larger crystals than extrusive forms (4 marks).
5. Sediments are weathered/eroded, transported and deposited; burial causes compaction and cementation. Chemical precipitation and biological accumulation also form sedimentary rocks (3 marks). Groups: clastic/mechanical, organic/biogenic, chemical (3 marks). Total 6.
6. Any three: often layered; grain size varies; may be soft or hard; fossils are often present; may be clastic, chemical or biogenic (3 marks). The statement is wrong because fossils are commonly preserved in sedimentary rocks (1 mark). Total 4.
7. Existing rock is changed by heat, pressure and/or hot fluids without complete melting (2 marks). Any three: slate, marble, quartzite, schist, gneiss (3 marks). Total 5.
8. Magma cools and solidifies into igneous rock; weathering/erosion create sediments; deposition followed by compaction/cementation forms sedimentary rock; heat and pressure form metamorphic rock; melting can return rock to magma (5 marks).
9. Any five valid uses from section 7 (5 marks).
10. Granite—igneous; sandstone—sedimentary; marble—metamorphic; basalt—igneous; chalk—sedimentary; gneiss—metamorphic; rock salt—sedimentary (7 marks, 1 each).

Total: 47 marks.

SOURCE QUESTION REVIEW
The source states that sedimentary rocks do not contain fossils. This is incorrect: fossils are commonly preserved in sedimentary rocks, including chalk and fossiliferous limestone. The source's list of organically formed rocks includes petroleum; petroleum is a liquid hydrocarbon fuel, not a solid rock. The source's final weekend question has two non-rock options (petrol and micro-organisms), so it cannot be scored as a single-answer multiple-choice question; a corrected replacement question is supplied. The source introduces metamorphic rocks in the classification but does not teach their formation or characteristics; this lesson supplies the missing strand.

SOURCES AND PROVENANCE
This is an original SS1 teaching supplement for the school's First Term Geography Week Eight topic. It corrects the fossil statement, distinguishes petroleum from solid rock, and supplies the missing metamorphic-rock strand. The original school document remains unchanged.
U.S. Geological Survey, What are metamorphic rocks?: https://www.usgs.gov/faqs/what-are-metamorphic-rocks (metamorphic process, examples, foliated/non-foliated rocks).
U.S. Geological Survey, Collecting Rocks: https://pubs.usgs.gov/gip/collect1/collectgip.html (rock types and metamorphic transformation without melting).
U.S. National Park Service, Rock ID — Teachers: https://www.nps.gov/teachers/classrooms/rock-id.htm (sedimentary rocks, fossils and rock classification).
U.S. National Park Service, Activity 1: Types of Rocks: https://www.nps.gov/choh/learn/kidsyouth/activity-1-types-of-rocks.htm (three rock groups and sedimentary formation).
The school's reading pointer 'Essential Geography, O.A. Iwena, pages 24-25' is recorded in the source, but the book was not supplied; those pages have not been inspected or independently verified.
