lessons.subject: Geography
lessons.title: Geographic Information Systems (GIS)
objectives: Define GIS and describe its common components and functions.
Explain discrete objects and continuous fields and distinguish raster from vector data.
Identify GIS layers, attributes and common spatial analyses.
Classify physical and cultural features and describe practical uses of GIS.
lessons.body:
GEOGRAPHIC INFORMATION SYSTEM (GIS)

Learning focus
By the end of this lesson, you should be able to define a geographic information system; explain how GIS stores, analyses and displays location-based data; distinguish raster and vector data; identify physical and cultural features; and give examples of how GIS can be used in everyday life and at school.

1. What is GIS?
A Geographic Information System (GIS) is a computer-based system for capturing, storing, managing, editing, analysing and displaying information linked to places on Earth. GIS combines geographic data (where something is) with descriptive information (what it is like). It is more than a digital map: it can compare layers of information, answer location-based questions and help people make decisions.

A GIS commonly involves:
- Hardware: computers, servers, GPS receivers, scanners and other devices.
- Software: applications used to enter, manage, analyse and display geographic data.
- Data: maps, satellite images, coordinates, measurements and descriptive records.
- People: the users who collect, maintain, interpret and apply the information.
- Methods: procedures and rules for collecting, checking, analysing and sharing data.

2. What information can GIS represent?
GIS represents real-world features and conditions that have a location. Examples include roads, buildings, schools, hospitals, rivers, lakes, forests, land use, soil types, rainfall and elevation.

Geographic features may be described as:
- Discrete objects: separate features with a clear identity or boundary, such as a school, house, road, bridge or lake.
- Continuous fields: values that vary across an area, such as rainfall, temperature, elevation or soil moisture.

3. Two common ways GIS stores spatial data
A. Vector data
Vector data represents features using coordinates and geometric shapes:
- Point: a single location, such as a borehole, school gate or clinic.
- Line: a feature with length, such as a road, river or pipeline.
- Polygon: a closed area, such as a school boundary, farm, lake or local government area.

Each vector feature can have an attribute record, for example a school name, road type, population or area.

B. Raster data
Raster data represents space as a grid of cells or pixels. Each cell stores a value, such as rainfall amount, elevation, temperature or a land-cover category. Raster is useful for continuous surfaces and for imagery from satellites or aerial photographs. A raster image is a way of storing data; GIS software can analyse raster data as well as display it.

4. GIS layers and attributes
A GIS map is often made from several layers. For example, a school-area map may contain:
1. A base map showing the area and major streets.
2. A point layer showing school buildings, gates and water points.
3. A line layer showing roads and footpaths.
4. A polygon layer showing the school boundary and playing fields.
5. A raster layer showing elevation or land cover.

An attribute table stores descriptive information linked to features. A point representing a classroom block could have attributes such as block name, number of rooms and condition. Layers can be switched on or off and compared to answer questions.

5. What can GIS do?
- Capture and store location-based data.
- Edit, update and manage geographic records.
- Search or query for features that meet stated conditions.
- Measure distance, area and location relationships.
- Overlay layers to compare different kinds of information.
- Analyse proximity, routes, patterns and changes over time.
- Display results as maps, tables, charts and reports.

6. Uses of GIS
- Urban and school planning: map schools, roads, public facilities and areas needing services.
- Transport: plan routes and analyse road networks and travel times.
- Disaster management: map flood-prone areas, evacuation routes and emergency facilities.
- Agriculture: map soil types, farm boundaries, rainfall and crop conditions.
- Health: map clinics and patterns of disease while protecting personal privacy.
- Environment: monitor forests, rivers, land use, erosion and pollution.
- Business and public services: identify where customers or services are located and plan suitable service areas.

7. Physical and cultural features
Physical features are natural parts of the environment, such as mountains, hills, valleys, rivers, lakes, forests, soils and natural vegetation.
Cultural (human-made) features are created or modified by people, such as roads, bridges, buildings, schools, airports, farms, dams, railways and settlements.
A feature's classification depends on what it is: a natural lake is physical; an artificial reservoir or dam is human-made. Trees are generally natural physical features, although a planted park or plantation is also shaped by people.

8. Geography and the word GIS
The word “geo” means Earth. “Graphy” relates to writing, description or representation. Geography is the study of places, environments and the relationships between people and the physical world. GIS supports geography by organising and analysing information tied to location.

9. Answers to the source general evaluation and weekend assignment
GIS is a computer-based system that captures, stores, manages, analyses and displays geographically referenced information.
Two features represented in GIS may be roads and rivers, or schools and elevation. Three cultural features include roads, bridges and buildings. Five physical features include mountains, rivers, lakes, valleys and forests.
The word “geo” refers to Earth.
Real objects may be represented as discrete objects or continuous fields. Raster data stores information in cells/pixels; vector data represents points, lines and polygons. A road is a cultural feature, while a mountain and river are physical features. An airport is a cultural/socio-economic feature; trees and lakes are physical features.

PRACTICE
1. Define GIS and explain why it is more than a digital map.
2. List the five common components of a GIS.
3. Explain the difference between a discrete object and a continuous field. Give two examples of each.
4. Distinguish vector data from raster data.
5. Give one GIS example each of a point, line and polygon feature.
6. List four uses of GIS in a school or local community.
7. State five physical features and five cultural features that could be mapped around your school or community.
8. Explain what an attribute table stores and how GIS layers can be used together.

ANSWER GUIDE
1. GIS is a computer-based system for capturing, storing, managing, analysing and displaying location-linked data (3 marks). It is more than a digital map because it can query, compare layers and analyse spatial relationships (2 marks). Total 5.
2. Hardware, software, data, people and methods/procedures (5 marks; 1 each).
3. Discrete objects are separate identifiable features (e.g. a school or house); continuous fields vary across an area (e.g. rainfall or elevation). Award 2 marks for the distinction and 1 mark for each of two examples (4 marks).
4. Vector uses points, lines and polygons; raster uses a grid of cells/pixels storing values (4 marks). Accept one correct use/example for each for up to 2 additional marks. Total 6.
5. Point—school gate; line—road; polygon—school boundary (3 marks).
6. Any four: map buildings and facilities; plan safe routes; map drainage/flood risk; manage school assets; plan transport; locate nearby health or emergency services (4 marks).
7. Five valid physical features (5 marks) and five valid cultural features (5 marks). Total 10.
8. An attribute table stores descriptive data linked to a geographic feature (2 marks). Layers can be overlaid/compared to analyse how features relate (2 marks). Total 4.

Total: 41 marks.

SOURCE QUESTION REVIEW
The source distinguishes discrete objects from continuous fields and names raster and vector as storage methods. The lesson clarifies that vector geometry includes points, lines and polygons, while raster uses grid cells/pixels. The two embedded Wikipedia hyperlinks in the source are not used as authority in this supplement; current definitions and data-model explanations are attributed to USGS and the Federal Geographic Data Committee. The source's wording “real objects” is retained conceptually but the lesson explains that GIS can represent both separate objects and continuous fields.

SOURCES AND PROVENANCE
This is an original SS1 teaching supplement for the school's First Term Geography Week Nine topic. It expands the source's short definition and data-representation notes into beginner-level explanations, local examples and keyed assessment. The original school document remains unchanged.
U.S. Geological Survey, What is a geographic information system (GIS)?: https://www.usgs.gov/faqs/what-a-geographic-information-system-gis (definition and examples of GIS analysis).
U.S. Geological Survey, GIS Educational Resources: https://www.usgs.gov/centers/wetland-and-aquatic-research-center/science/usgs-geographic-information-systems-gis (vector/raster data, points, lines, polygons, cells and layers).
Federal Geographic Data Committee, Terminology: https://www.fgdc.gov/initiatives/framework/handbook/appendixA (GIS and raster data model definitions).
The source contains two Wikipedia hyperlink fields; they are not used as supporting authority here. The school source is the topic and assessment reference.

lessons.subject: Geography
lessons.title: Major Landforms of the World: Mountains
objectives: Define mountains and highlands and distinguish the two terms.
Explain fold, block, volcanic and residual mountain formation.
Identify anticlines, synclines, horsts and grabens and give accurate examples.
Explain the advantages and disadvantages of mountains and draw a labelled formation diagram.
lessons.body:
MAJOR LANDFORMS OF THE WORLD: MOUNTAINS

Learning focus
By the end of this lesson, you should be able to define a mountain and a highland; identify four mountain types; explain how fold, block, volcanic and residual mountains form; identify anticlines, synclines, horsts and grabens; give examples; and explain the advantages and disadvantages of mountains.

1. What is a mountain?
A mountain is a high, elevated part of Earth's surface that rises noticeably above the surrounding land and usually has steep slopes and a summit or peak. Mountains may form through tectonic uplift, folding, faulting, volcanic activity or long-term erosion that leaves resistant rock standing above the surrounding landscape.

A highland is a broad area of land that is higher than the surrounding lowlands. It may include mountains, hills, plateaus and elevated valleys. Examples include the Ethiopian Highlands and the Highlands of Scotland. A highland is a general landform region; it is not necessarily a single mountain.

2. Fold mountains
Fold mountains form mainly where tectonic plates converge and compress layers of rock. The pressure shortens and thickens the crust and bends rock layers into folds. The upward arch of a fold is an anticline; the downward trough is a syncline. Some folds may be tilted, overturned or pushed over other rocks along thrust faults.

Simple fold model
Before compression:  ─────────────── rock layers
Compression:          → → →     ← ← ←
After folding:         ∩  ∪  ∩  ∪
                       anticline / syncline

Characteristics include folded rock layers, long mountain ranges, steep slopes and high peaks. The rocks may be hard or weak depending on their composition; it is not correct to describe all fold mountains as soft. Fold mountains are not necessarily volcanic, although volcanic activity may occur near some convergent plate boundaries.

Examples include the Himalayas, Alps and Atlas Mountains. The Andes include complex mountain-building processes along a convergent margin and should not be treated as a simple example of only one process.

3. Block mountains
Block mountains form when the Earth's crust breaks along faults and large blocks move up or down. They are commonly associated with tensional forces that pull the crust apart, although faulting can also occur under compression.

A raised block between faults is called a horst; a down-dropped block is called a graben. A graben may form a rift valley. The East African Rift System contains long rift valleys and associated fault-block landscapes.

Simple block model
Crust pulled apart:       ←           →
Faults form:              \           /
Raised block (horst):       ┌─────┐
Down-dropped block (graben): └─____┘

Characteristics include steep faulted sides and relatively flat or gently sloping tops in some examples. Examples include the Ruwenzori Mountains of East Africa, the Vosges and the Black Forest in Europe. A rift valley is associated with fault-block structures; the raised blocks are horsts and the down-dropped blocks are grabens.

4. Volcanic mountains
Volcanic mountains form when magma rises through vents or cracks and erupts as lava, ash, cinders and other volcanic materials. Repeated eruptions deposit material around a vent and may build a cone-shaped mountain. These are sometimes called mountains of accumulation because erupted material builds up the landform.

Simple volcanic model
             crater
              /\
             /  \       layers of lava and ash
            /    \
           /  |   \
          /   |    \
              |       central vent
          magma chamber

Characteristics include a cone or dome shape, a crater or vent in many examples, and layers of lava and fragmented volcanic material. The shape depends on the type of magma, eruption style and erosion.

Examples include Mount Fuji in Japan, Mayon in the Philippines, Mount Kilimanjaro, Mount Kenya, Mount Elgon and Mount Cameroon in Africa. Mount Ruwenzori is a fault-block mountain, not a volcanic mountain; the source's list incorrectly places it with volcanoes.

5. Residual mountains
Residual mountains are the resistant remains of older highlands or mountain ranges that have been worn down by denudation. Denudation includes weathering, erosion and the removal of material by rivers, wind, ice and mass movement. Softer surrounding rocks are removed more quickly, leaving harder rock as isolated hills, ridges or peaks. These are sometimes called mountains of denudation.

Simple residual model
Original highland:       /^^^^^^^^^^\
Long erosion:            ↓ ↓ ↓ ↓ ↓ ↓
Remaining resistant rock:      /\
                               /  \

Examples include Mount Monadnock in the United States and parts of the Highlands of Scotland and Scandinavia. The Deccan Plateau is a plateau, not a single residual mountain; do not use it as a precise example of a residual mountain.

6. Advantages and disadvantages of mountains
Advantages
- They are sources of minerals and some other natural resources.
- They can encourage orographic rainfall when moist air is forced to rise and cool.
- They provide water catchments and sources of rivers.
- They offer sites for hydroelectric power where suitable rivers and relief occur.
- They support tourism, recreation and cultural activities.
- They provide habitats and biodiversity and may act as climatic barriers or wind-breaks.
- Mountain grasslands may support transhumance, the seasonal movement of livestock between grazing areas.

Disadvantages and challenges
- Steep slopes and rugged relief can make roads, railways and communication difficult and expensive.
- Some high-altitude areas have harsh weather and limited settlement or farming opportunities.
- Steep or poorly managed slopes may be affected by soil erosion, landslides and rockfalls.
- Thin or infertile soils occur in some mountain areas, although soil quality varies and is not universally poor.
- Mountains can isolate communities and increase the cost of delivering services.

7. Answers to the source evaluation and theory questions
Three mountain types are fold, block and volcanic (residual is also a type).
A block mountain is also called a horst when a block is raised between faults.
Rift valleys are associated with faulting and block mountains; a down-dropped block is a graben.
Volcanic and residual mountains are also called mountains of accumulation and mountains of denudation respectively.
Two volcanic mountain examples include Mount Fuji and Mount Kilimanjaro; other acceptable examples are Mayon, Mount Kenya, Mount Elgon and Mount Cameroon.
Four advantages include mineral resources, rainfall/water catchments, hydroelectric power and tourism. Other valid points are biodiversity, transhumance and climatic barriers.
A highland is an elevated region above surrounding lowlands. Examples include the Ethiopian Highlands and Highlands of Scotland.

PRACTICE
1. Define a mountain and a highland.
2. Name the four main mountain types and state the process that forms each.
3. Explain the formation of fold mountains. Define anticline and syncline.
4. Explain the formation of block mountains. Define horst and graben.
5. Describe how a volcanic mountain forms and give three examples.
6. Explain how residual mountains form and give two examples.
7. State four advantages and three disadvantages of mountains.
8. Explain the meaning of transhumance and state why mountain grasslands may support it.
9. With a labelled diagram, explain the formation of one type of mountain.

ANSWER GUIDE
1. Mountain: high land rising noticeably above surrounding land, usually with steep slopes and a peak (2 marks). Highland: broad elevated region above surrounding lowlands (2 marks). Total 4.
2. Fold—compression and folding; block—faulting and movement of crustal blocks; volcanic—accumulation of lava/ash around vents; residual—denudation leaves resistant rock (4 marks, 1 each).
3. Converging plates compress and fold rock layers; anticline is an upfold and syncline is a downfold (4 marks: formation 2, terms 2).
4. Faults form and blocks move up or down; horst is a raised block and graben is a down-dropped block (4 marks: formation 2, terms 2).
5. Magma erupts as lava/ash/cinders; repeated deposits build a cone or other volcanic landform (2 marks). Any three examples (3 marks). Total 5.
6. Weathering and erosion remove weaker surrounding material, leaving resistant remnants (2 marks). Any two valid examples, such as Mount Monadnock and Highlands of Scotland (2 marks). Total 4.
7. Any four advantages (4 marks) and any three disadvantages (3 marks). Total 7.
8. Transhumance is seasonal movement of livestock between grazing areas (2 marks); mountain grasslands may provide seasonal pasture (1 mark). Total 3.
9. Award 2 marks for correct process, 3 marks for labelled features and sequence, and 1 mark for a clear title/key (6 marks).

Total: 41 marks.

SOURCE QUESTION REVIEW
The source describes fold mountains as soft and says they are noted for active volcanoes; neither is a defining property of all fold mountains. The source lists Ruwenzori among volcanic mountains, but it is a fault-block mountain. The source lists the Deccan Plateau as a residual mountain; a plateau is a broad elevated landform, not a single residual mountain. “Mount Manodnock” is corrected to Mount Monadnock. The source's “unfolds of wrinkles” question is interpreted as upfolds (anticlines) and downfolds (synclines). The source's lists of advantages/disadvantages are preserved but clarified so that soil quality and settlement limits are not stated as universal rules.

SOURCES AND PROVENANCE
This is an original SS1 teaching supplement for the school's First Term Geography Week Ten topic. It preserves the four mountain types and assessment objectives while correcting examples and adding student-readable process diagrams and a complete marking guide. The original school document remains unchanged.
U.S. National Park Service, Tectonic Landforms and Mountain Building: https://www.nps.gov/subjects/geology/tectonic-landforms.htm (fold mountains, fault-block mountains, horsts and grabens, volcanic mountains).
U.S. National Park Service, Mountain Building Lesson Plan: https://www.nps.gov/teachers/classrooms/mountain-building-lesson.htm (compression, folding, extension and fault blocks).
U.S. Geological Survey, What is a fault and what are the different types?: https://www.usgs.gov/faqs/what-a-fault-and-what-are-different-types (normal and reverse fault movement).
U.S. National Park Service, Erosional Volcanic Landforms: https://www.nps.gov/subjects/volcanoes/erosional-volcanic-landforms.htm (volcanic construction and subsequent erosion).
The school's reading pointer 'Essential Geography, O.A. Iwena, pages 31-33' is recorded in the source, but the book was not supplied; those pages have not been inspected or independently verified.

lessons.title: Introduction to Geography: Nature, Meaning, Scope and Value
objectives: Explain the nature of geography as an integrative study of places, environments and spatial relationships.
Define geography and explain the meaning of geo and graphy.
Describe the scope of physical and human geography.
Explain the value of geography to people and society.
lessons.body:
INTRODUCTION TO GEOGRAPHY: NATURE, MEANING, SCOPE AND VALUE

Learning focus
By the end of this lesson, you should be able to explain the nature of geography; define geography; explain the meaning of “geo” and “graphy”; describe the scope of geography; and explain why geography is useful to individuals and society.

1. The nature of geography
Geography is the study of places, environments and the relationships between people and the Earth. It asks where things are, why they are there, how places are connected and how people and environments affect one another. Geography is spatial because it studies location, distribution, distance, movement and patterns across places. It is integrative because it connects physical processes with human activities. It is also dynamic because environments, populations, settlements and economies change over time.

Geography has two broad, connected areas:
- Physical geography studies natural features and processes, such as landforms, rocks, rivers, oceans, weather, climate, soils and vegetation.
- Human geography studies people and their activities, such as population, settlements, agriculture, mining, trade, transport, manufacturing, culture and the use of resources.

Environmental and regional geography bring these areas together. For example, a geographer may study how rainfall and soil affect farming, how a river influences settlement, or how road construction changes a landscape. Geography is therefore not only the description of the Earth's surface and is not only a social science; it draws on both natural and social sciences.

2. Meaning of geography
The word “geography” comes from Greek roots: geo means Earth and graphia relates to writing or description. Geography was traditionally described as the description of the Earth. Modern geography goes further: it studies the Earth's physical and human features, the distribution of these features, the processes that shape them and the relationships between people and their environments.

3. Scope of geography
The scope of geography is broad. It includes:
- The Earth as a planet, including its size, shape, movements and position in the solar system.
- Landforms and rocks, including mountains, plains, valleys and the processes that shape them.
- Water bodies, including oceans, seas, rivers, lakes and the water cycle.
- Weather, climate, rainfall and the atmosphere.
- Soils, vegetation, animals and natural resources.
- People, population, settlements, occupations and economic activities such as farming, fishing, mining, trade, manufacturing and construction.
- Culture, transport, communication, land use and the distribution of services.
- The location, distribution, movement and interaction of natural and human features from local to global scales.

Geography is connected with other subjects. For example, it uses mathematics for scale and measurement; biology for ecosystems; chemistry for soils and water; physics for weather and energy; and economics, history and government for human activities and development. Geography connects these ideas through their location and relationship to place.

4. Value and importance of geography
Geography is useful because it:
1. Helps people understand their local environment and the wider world.
2. Explains environmental and social problems and supports informed solutions.
3. Builds knowledge of the ways of life, cultures and activities of people in different places.
4. Supports town, rural, regional, transport and economic planning.
5. Helps people understand climate, vegetation, rivers, soils, oceans, mountains and other physical features.
6. Connects knowledge from other subjects and helps people understand how different processes work together.
7. Supports careers in teaching, surveying, mapping, GIS, urban and regional planning, environmental management, transport, agriculture, disaster management and research.

5. How geography helps in everyday decisions
A farmer may use information about rainfall, soil and slope to select crops. A town planner may use maps to decide where roads, schools and clinics should be located. A family may use weather information to prepare for heavy rain. A community may study flood risk before building houses. These examples show that geography is practical as well as academic.

PRACTICE
1. Explain the nature of geography in your own words.
2. Distinguish physical geography from human geography and give two examples of each.
3. Explain the meaning of the words “geo” and “graphy”.
4. State five areas covered by the scope of geography.
5. Explain four ways geography is useful to society.
6. Give two examples of how geographical knowledge can help people make decisions in everyday life.

ANSWER GUIDE
1. Geography studies places, environments, spatial patterns and relationships between people and the Earth. Award up to 3 marks for location/distribution, physical-human relationships and change/processes.
2. Physical geography studies natural features/processes (e.g. rivers, climate); human geography studies people and activities (e.g. settlements, farming). Award 2 marks for the distinction and 1 mark for each of two suitable examples (4 marks).
3. Geo means Earth; graphia relates to writing or description (2 marks).
4. Any five accurate areas from section 3 (5 marks).
5. Any four valid values from section 4 (4 marks).
6. Any two practical examples with a clear decision link, such as farming and rainfall/soil, town planning and facility location, or flood preparation and weather/risk information (4 marks).

Total: 22 marks.

SOURCE AND SCOPE NOTE
The original Week One source provides meaning, scope and value but does not teach the “nature of geography” named in the scheme row. This lesson supplies that missing teaching. It retains the source's topic sequence and improves the definition by explaining geography as an integrative study of physical and human environments. The reading assignment “Essential Geography, O.A. Iwena, pages 1-2” is recorded in the source, but the book was not supplied; those pages have not been inspected or independently verified.

lessons.body:
WEEK ONE: SOURCE EVALUATION AND ASSESSMENT — ANSWERS AND MARKING GUIDE

This assessment guide answers the questions printed in the school's First Term Geography Week One source. It is a companion to the lesson “Introduction to Geography: Nature, Meaning, Scope and Value”.

A. Evaluation questions
1. What is Geography?
Answer: Geography is the study of places, the Earth's physical and human features, their location and distribution, and the relationships between people and their environment.
2. The Greek word “Geo” means what?
Answer: Earth.
3. Explain the scope of geography.
Answer: The scope includes the Earth as a planet; landforms and rocks; water bodies; weather and climate; soils and vegetation; animals and natural resources; population, settlements, occupations and economic activities; culture, transport, communication and the spatial distribution and interaction of human and physical features.
4. What are the values of Geography?
Answer: Geography helps people understand their environment and other places; identify and solve environmental and social problems; understand other people's ways of life; support urban, rural, regional and economic planning; understand physical features and processes; connect knowledge from other subjects; and prepare for careers such as teaching, surveying, GIS, planning and environmental management.

B. General evaluation
1. What is Geography? See answer A1.
2. Explain the scope of Geography. See answer A3.
3. What are the importance of Geography in our society? Give any four or more points from answer A4.
4. “Geo” in the word Geography means what? Earth.
5. The capital of Lagos State is Ikeja.

C. Weekend assignment — multiple choice
1. “_____ is defined as the description of the Earth.” Correct answer: (c) Geography.
2. “One of the following is wrong about Geography.” Correct answer: (b) it helps us to study temperature and rainfall of places only. Geography studies more than weather; it also studies land, water, people, activities and their relationships.
3. “Geography is a social science subject which deals with the study of …” Intended answer: (b) man and his environment. Modern geography also includes physical geography and therefore draws on natural sciences.
4. “Geography cuts across the following other fields of human study except …” The source's intended answer is (c) Music, because the other options are the cross-curricular examples explicitly listed in the source. However, the source's scope list ends with “etc.” and cultural geography can study music as a cultural activity. Treat this as a provisional school-text answer and do not use it for high-stakes marking until the teacher confirms the intended scope.
5. “Geo” in Greek means … Correct answer: (c) Earth.

D. Theory
1. Write the capitals of these Nigerian states:
- Ebonyi State — Abakaliki.
- Plateau State — Jos.
- Ogun State — Abeokuta.
2. State two importance of Geography.
Answer: Any two well-explained points, such as understanding the environment; supporting planning; helping solve environmental problems; understanding other places and cultures; or preparing people for careers in mapping, GIS, planning, teaching and environmental management.

E. Marking guide for a 30-mark class assessment
1. Define Geography accurately (4 marks): study of places/Earth (2); physical and human features (1); spatial relationships/environment interaction (1).
2. Explain the scope (6 marks): award 1 mark each for six distinct, accurate areas.
3. State four values of Geography (4 marks): 1 mark each.
4. State the meaning of geo and graphy (2 marks): geo = Earth (1); graphy = writing/description (1).
5. State the four capitals asked in Week One (4 marks): Lagos—Ikeja; Ebonyi—Abakaliki; Plateau—Jos; Ogun—Abeokuta (1 each). The separate capitals supplement teaches these four only; it is not a full state-capitals syllabus.
6. Answer the five source multiple-choice questions (5 marks): 1 mark each. Question 4 (Music) is provisional and requires teacher confirmation before it is scored.
7. State two importance of Geography (4 marks): 2 marks per well-explained point.
8. Presentation and clarity (1 mark).
Total: 30 marks. If the teacher withholds the provisional Music item, award the remaining 29 marks and adjust the total accordingly.

F. Teacher review note
The source's Week One reading pointer has not been checked against the textbook because the book was not supplied. The Music multiple-choice item is answered according to the likely intended key but is not logically exclusive because the source uses “etc.” in its list of connected subjects. Teacher confirmation is required before that one item is scored. The rest of the source questions have a clear answer or marking criterion.

lessons.subject: Geography
lessons.title: Plateaus
objectives: Define plateaus and describe their main features.
Explain tectonic, volcanic and dissected plateau formation.
Distinguish tablelands, intermontane plateaus, mesas and buttes.
Explain plateau uses and disadvantages and answer the source assessment.
lessons.body:
PLATEAUS

Learning focus
By the end of this lesson, you should be able to define a plateau; describe its main features; explain tectonic, volcanic and dissected plateaus; distinguish tablelands from intermontane plateaus; give examples; and explain the uses and disadvantages of plateaus.

1. What is a plateau?
A plateau is an extensive area of elevated land with a generally level or gently rolling surface. It stands higher than the surrounding land and commonly has a steep slope or escarpment along at least one side. A plateau may have deep valleys, irregular surfaces, mesas and buttes. It is sometimes called a tableland because parts of its surface may be flat. Not every plateau is perfectly flat, and many have been cut by erosion.

2. Main types of plateaus
A. Tectonic plateaus
Tectonic plateaus form when broad areas of the Earth's crust are uplifted by movements within the Earth. The uplifted area may be relatively level or gently undulating. Some tectonic plateaus are enclosed by mountain ranges; these are called intermontane plateaus. A broad tableland is another common form of plateau surface.

Examples include the Tibetan Plateau, which lies between major mountain ranges, and the Altiplano of the Andes in South America. The Deccan Plateau in India is mainly a volcanic plateau, not a tectonic plateau. Do not use the source's unclear references to Harz and “Mesetal Liberia” as standard examples without teacher verification.

B. Volcanic or lava plateaus
Volcanic plateaus form when large quantities of fluid lava erupt from long cracks or many vents and spread over wide areas. The lava cools and solidifies in successive layers, gradually building an extensive elevated surface. They are also called lava plateaus.

Examples include the Deccan Plateau of India, the Columbia Plateau in the northwestern United States and the Antrim Plateau in Northern Ireland.

C. Dissected plateaus
A dissected plateau is an elevated area that has been deeply cut by rivers and other agents of erosion. Weathering and running water carve valleys and gorges into the plateau, leaving ridges, steep-sided remnants and irregular surfaces. Uplift may also contribute to the relief.

The school source lists the Jos Plateau in Nigeria, the Fouta Djallon region in Guinea and the Kumasi Plateau in Ghana as examples. The Jos Plateau has a complex geological history and includes volcanic features; retain the source's classification for its exercise, but do not assume all of its landforms have a single origin.

3. Related plateau features
- Tableland: a broad, elevated area with a relatively level top.
- Intermontane plateau: an elevated plateau enclosed by mountain ranges.
- Mesa: an isolated, flat-topped hill or small plateau with steep sides.
- Butte: a smaller, steep-sided, flat-topped hill, usually narrower than a mesa.
- Escarpment: a long, steep slope or cliff separating areas of different elevation.

4. Uses and importance of plateaus
- Some plateaus contain minerals such as tin, gold and other valuable ores.
- Their scenery, waterfalls and unusual landforms may attract tourists.
- Some are sources of rivers and water for communities and agriculture.
- Cooler conditions at higher elevations may favour settlement in some regions.
- Suitable soils and climates can support specialised farming and crop production.
- Grasslands may support cattle, sheep and goat rearing.

5. Disadvantages and challenges
- Steep edges, deep valleys and rugged surfaces can make road, railway and airport construction difficult and expensive.
- Erosion may remove soil and make farming difficult on exposed slopes.
- Some plateau areas have limited water, thin soils or harsh conditions; this varies by location.
- Isolated communities may face higher transport and service-delivery costs.

6. Solar-system fact used in the source evaluation
The source's general evaluation asks students to list nine planets. The current recognised number is eight: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune. Pluto is classified as a dwarf planet, not one of the eight planets.

7. Answers to the source evaluation and weekend assignment
A plateau is an extensive elevated area with a generally level or gently rolling surface, commonly with a steep side.
A tectonic plateau forms through broad uplift of the Earth's crust. The two forms named in the source are tableland and intermontane plateau.
A plateau is regarded as dissected when rivers and other agents of denudation have cut deep valleys into it, leaving an irregular surface. The source examples are Jos Plateau, Fouta Djallon and Kumasi Plateau.
Two advantages include mineral resources, tourism, river sources, farming, grazing and settlement. Two disadvantages include difficult transport construction and erosion.
Weekend answers: (1) intermontane plateau; (2) dissected plateau; (3) dissected plateau according to the source's classification; (4) volcanic/lava plateau; (5) Columbia Plateau (the source's “Columbia Snake” wording is standardised to Columbia Plateau).

PRACTICE
1. Define a plateau and state three features that distinguish it from a plain.
2. Explain how a tectonic plateau forms. What is an intermontane plateau?
3. Explain how a volcanic plateau forms and give three examples.
4. Explain how a dissected plateau forms and give three examples from the school source.
5. Distinguish a mesa from a butte.
6. State four uses or advantages of plateaus.
7. State three disadvantages or challenges associated with plateaus.
8. List the eight recognised planets in order from the Sun and explain the status of Pluto.

ANSWER GUIDE
1. A plateau is an extensive elevated area with a generally level or gently rolling surface (2 marks). Features may include higher elevation, steep edges/escarpments, broad summit surface and deeply cut valleys (3 marks). Total 5.
2. Broad crustal uplift raises an extensive area (2 marks). An intermontane plateau is enclosed by mountain ranges (2 marks). Total 4.
3. Lava spreads over a wide area in repeated flows and solidifies in layers (2 marks). Examples: Deccan, Columbia and Antrim plateaus (3 marks). Total 5.
4. Rivers and other erosional agents cut valleys and gorges into an elevated area (2 marks). School-source examples: Jos, Fouta Djallon and Kumasi (3 marks). Total 5.
5. A mesa is a larger flat-topped, steep-sided remnant; a butte is smaller and usually narrower (2 marks).
6. Any four: minerals, tourism, river sources, settlement, farming, pasture and livestock (4 marks).
7. Any three: difficult transport construction, erosion, limited water/thin soils in some areas, isolation and higher service costs (3 marks).
8. Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune (4 marks for correct order). Pluto is a dwarf planet (1 mark). Total 5.

Total: 33 marks.

SOURCE QUESTION REVIEW
The source classifies the Deccan Plateau as tectonic, but it is widely recognised as a volcanic plateau formed by extensive lava flows. The source's “Columbia Snake Plateau” is standardised to the Columbia Plateau. The source's “Mesetal Liberia” and Harz examples are unclear or not reliable examples of tectonic plateaus and are not used as keyed examples. The source's general evaluation asks for nine planets; the current recognised count is eight, with Pluto classified as a dwarf planet since 2006. Jos Plateau is retained as a school-source example of a dissected plateau, with a note that its geological history is complex.

SOURCES AND PROVENANCE
This is an original SS1 teaching supplement for the school's Second Term Geography Week Two topic. It corrects plateau examples and the obsolete planet count while retaining the source's three plateau types and assessment objectives. The original school document remains unchanged.
U.S. National Park Service, Plateaus and Mesas: https://www.nps.gov/subjects/nnlandmarks/plateaus-and-mesas.htm (plateau definition, formation processes, mesas and erosion).
U.S. Geological Survey, Plateaus: https://apps.usgs.gov/thesaurus/term-simple.php?code=832&thcode=3 (plateau definition and geomorphic characteristics).
NASA, About the Planets: https://science.nasa.gov/solar-system/planets/ (eight recognised planets and Pluto's dwarf-planet classification).
The school's reading pointer 'Essential Geography, pages 34-35' is recorded in the source, but the book was not supplied; those pages have not been inspected or independently verified.

practice.question: Explain how a dissected plateau forms and give three examples from the school source.
practice.answer: Rivers and other erosional agents cut valleys and gorges into an elevated area. School-source examples: Jos, Fouta Djallon and Kumasi.

practice.question: Distinguish a mesa from a butte.
practice.answer: A mesa is a larger flat-topped, steep-sided remnant; a butte is smaller and usually narrower.

practice.question: State four uses or advantages of plateaus.
practice.answer: Any four: minerals, tourism, river sources, settlement, farming, pasture and livestock.

practice.question: State three disadvantages or challenges associated with plateaus.
practice.answer: Any three: difficult transport construction, erosion, limited water/thin soils in some areas, isolation and higher service costs.

practice.question: List the eight recognised planets in order from the Sun and explain the status of Pluto.
practice.answer: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune. Pluto is a dwarf planet.

lessons.subject: Geography
lessons.title: Lowlands and Plains
objectives: Define plains and describe their main characteristics.
Explain structural, erosional and depositional plains.
Describe the main types of depositional plains and distinguish peneplains from pediplains.
Explain the uses and disadvantages of plains and answer the source assessment.
lessons.body:
LOWLANDS AND PLAINS

Learning focus
By the end of this lesson, you should be able to define a plain; explain structural, erosional and depositional plains; describe the main types of depositional plains; distinguish a peneplain from a pediplain; and explain the uses and disadvantages of plains.

1. What is a plain?
A plain is an extensive area of land with a level or gently undulating surface and relatively little local relief. Many plains are low-lying, but not every plain is only a few metres above sea level; some are elevated. Plains may form through the structure of underlying rocks, long-term erosion or the deposition of sediments.

2. Main types of plains
A. Structural plains
Structural plains are broad, relatively level areas where sedimentary rock layers remain mostly horizontal or have been gently uplifted. They have not been strongly folded or faulted. The Russian Platform and the Great Plains of the United States are examples commonly used in school geography classifications. The Great Plains include varied sedimentary deposits and landforms, so the label is a broad regional classification.

B. Erosional plains
Erosional plains form when weathering and denudation wear down higher or uneven land over long periods. Rivers, wind, rain, waves and glaciers can remove material and reduce relief.

Two important erosional surfaces are:
- Peneplain: a nearly level surface produced by prolonged erosion, especially by rivers, that reduces an old land surface close to a low-relief condition.
- Pediplain: a broad, gently sloping surface formed when pediments at the bases of hills or mountains expand and join, commonly in dry or semi-arid regions through slope retreat and erosion. It is not simply a plain made by wind alone.

Examples in the school source include the Canadian Shield and desert surfaces called reg and hamada. These are broad erosional surfaces, though their exact landform classification depends on local geology and scale.

C. Depositional plains
Depositional plains form when transported sediments are laid down by rivers, wind, waves, glaciers or in lakes. As deposits accumulate, they may build broad, relatively level surfaces.

Main types of depositional plains
1. Alluvial plains: formed from river-deposited sand, silt, clay and gravel. They may include floodplains and alluvial fans.
2. Floodplains: low, relatively flat land beside a river channel that may be covered by water when the river overflows its banks. Floodplains often have fertile soils but can be exposed to flood risk.
3. Deltaic plains: nearly level land at or near a river mouth, built by sediment deposited where the river enters a lake or sea. Deltas commonly contain branching distributary channels and wetlands.
4. Outwash plains: formed in front of glaciers when meltwater streams spread and deposit sorted glacial sediment.
5. Aeolian plains: formed by wind-deposited material such as sand or fine dust (loess).
6. Lacustrine plains: formed from sediments deposited on the bed of a former lake or in a lake basin.
7. Coastal plains: low-lying areas along a coast formed or modified by marine deposition, changes in sea level and coastal processes.

3. Uses and importance of plains
- Level or gently sloping land often makes settlement and construction easier.
- Fertile alluvial and other depositional soils can support intensive agriculture.
- Plains often provide routes for roads, railways and airports, where drainage and ground conditions are suitable.
- Rivers and wetlands can supply water, support fishing and provide transport routes.
- Some plains contain mineral and energy resources, including coal and petroleum-bearing formations.
- Grasslands in suitable climates can support grazing and livestock rearing.

4. Disadvantages and challenges of plains
- Floodplains and deltaic plains may be inundated during floods, damaging homes, farms and infrastructure.
- Poor drainage can cause waterlogging and make some land difficult to cultivate or build on.
- Wetlands, rivers and seasonal watercourses may require bridges, culverts and drainage works, increasing construction costs.
- Arid plains may experience drought, wind erosion and limited water for farming.
- Open plains may offer little natural shelter from strong winds or extreme weather.

5. Effects of Earth's rotation
Earth rotates from west to east about its axis once in approximately 24 hours. Important effects include:
- Alternation of day and night as different parts of Earth face towards or away from the Sun.
- The apparent daily movement of the Sun, Moon and stars across the sky from east to west.
- Differences in local time from one longitude to another.
- The Coriolis effect, which deflects moving air and water to the right in the Northern Hemisphere and to the left in the Southern Hemisphere.
- A slight equatorial bulge and polar flattening because of rotation.

6. Answers to the source evaluation and weekend questions
A plain is an extensive area with a level or gently undulating surface.
The three main types in the source are structural, erosional and depositional plains.
Five depositional types include alluvial, flood, deltaic, outwash, aeolian, lacustrine and coastal plains (any five).
Structural plains have relatively undisturbed horizontal rock layers; erosional plains are worn down by denudation.
Earth's rotation causes day and night, apparent daily movement of celestial bodies, local-time differences, the Coriolis effect and equatorial bulging.
Weekend answers: (1) plain; (2) outwash plains; (3) erosional plains; (4) pediplain; (5) structural plains according to the school source.
Theory: a peneplain is a low-relief surface produced by prolonged erosion; a pediplain is formed as pediments expand and join, commonly in arid or semi-arid regions. Four disadvantages include flooding, waterlogging, costly drainage/bridges and drought or wind erosion in dry regions.

PRACTICE
1. Define a plain and state two characteristics.
2. Explain how structural plains form and give two examples.
3. Explain how erosional plains form. Distinguish a peneplain from a pediplain.
4. Explain how depositional plains form and name five types.
5. Describe the formation of a floodplain and a deltaic plain.
6. Explain how an outwash plain forms.
7. State four advantages and four disadvantages of plains.
8. Explain four effects of Earth's rotation.

ANSWER GUIDE
1. A plain is an extensive area with a level or gently undulating surface (2 marks); any two features such as low relief, broad extent or gentle slopes (2 marks). Total 4.
2. Structural plains are broad level areas with mostly horizontal or gently uplifted rock layers (2 marks). Examples: Russian Platform and Great Plains of the USA (2 marks). Total 4.
3. Erosion and denudation wear down uneven land over long periods (2 marks). Peneplain: prolonged erosion reduces relief; pediplain: pediments expand and join, commonly in dry/semi-arid regions (4 marks). Total 6.
4. Sediment is deposited by rivers, wind, waves, glaciers or in lakes (2 marks). Any five: alluvial, flood, deltaic, outwash, aeolian, lacustrine, coastal (5 marks). Total 7.
5. Floodplain forms from river deposits beside a channel and may be flooded when the river overtops its banks (2 marks). Deltaic plain forms from sediment deposited at a river mouth as the river enters standing water (2 marks). Total 4.
6. Meltwater streams in front of a glacier transport and deposit sorted sediment, building a broad, gently sloping plain (3 marks).
7. Any four advantages (4 marks) and any four disadvantages (4 marks). Total 8.
8. Any four: day/night; apparent daily movement; local-time differences; Coriolis deflection; equatorial bulge/polar flattening (4 marks).

Total: 40 marks.

SOURCE QUESTION REVIEW
The source's description of all plains as only a few metres above sea level is too narrow; elevated plains also exist. The source describes pediplains as formed when wind reduces highlands; the replacement explains the more accurate process of pediment expansion and slope retreat in dry regions. The source's Great Plains example is retained as a school classification. The source's question on Earth's rotation is outside the immediate plains topic but is answered rather than omitted.

SOURCES AND PROVENANCE
This is an original SS1 teaching supplement for the school's Second Term Geography Weeks Three and Four topic. It retains the three source classes and all assessment strands while adding accurate explanations of depositional plains, peneplains and pediplains. The original school document remains unchanged.
U.S. National Park Service, Outwash Plains and Eskers: https://www.nps.gov/articles/outwashplainsandeskers.htm (glacial meltwater and outwash deposition).
U.S. Geological Survey, Delta Plain: https://apps.usgs.gov/thesaurus/term-simple.php?code=GC-080&thcode=62 (delta-plain definition).
U.S. Geological Survey, Water Resources Glossary: https://water.usgs.gov/water-basics_glossary.html (floodplain definition).
U.S. Geological Survey, National Water Summary Glossary: https://water.usgs.gov/nwsum/WSP2425/glossary.html (delta and floodplain terms).
The school's reading pointer 'Essential Geography, pages 35-36' is recorded in the source, but the book was not supplied; those pages have not been inspected or independently verified.

lessons.subject: Geography
lessons.title: The Environment and Ecosystems
objectives: Define environment and ecosystem and distinguish biotic from abiotic components.
Explain the roles of producers, consumers and decomposers.
Describe interdependence, food chains and food webs.
Explain water, carbon, nitrogen and mineral cycles and how they support environmental balance.
lessons.body:
THE ENVIRONMENT AND ECOSYSTEMS

Learning focus
By the end of this lesson, you should be able to define environment and ecosystem; distinguish biotic and abiotic components; describe producers, consumers and decomposers; explain how living and non-living components depend on one another; and describe the water, carbon, nitrogen and mineral cycles.

1. What is the environment?
The environment is the total set of living and non-living conditions surrounding an organism or community. It includes natural features such as air, water, soil, sunlight, climate, plants and animals, as well as human-made features such as buildings, roads, farms and industries. The environment provides the resources and conditions needed for life and human activities.

The environment can be considered through four interacting Earth spheres:
- Lithosphere: the solid outer part of Earth, including rocks and soil.
- Hydrosphere: water on, under and above Earth's surface.
- Atmosphere: the layer of gases surrounding Earth.
- Biosphere: the parts of land, water and air where life exists.

2. What is an ecosystem?
An ecosystem is a community of living organisms interacting with one another and with the non-living environment in a particular area. A pond, forest, grassland, river, mangrove swamp or farm can be an ecosystem. An ecosystem includes both biotic and abiotic components and the processes that connect them.

3. Components of an ecosystem
A. Biotic (living) components
Biotic components are living organisms. They are commonly grouped by their roles in obtaining energy and nutrients.

Producers (autotrophs)
Green plants, algae and some bacteria make organic food from simpler substances. Most green plants use sunlight, water and carbon dioxide in photosynthesis. Producers form the base of most food chains.

Consumers (heterotrophs)
Consumers obtain energy by eating plants or other organisms. Primary consumers feed on producers; secondary consumers feed on primary consumers; tertiary consumers feed on secondary consumers. Humans, other animals and many parasites are consumers. Parasites obtain nutrients from a host, but they are not the only type of consumer.

Decomposers and detritivores
Bacteria and fungi break down dead organisms and wastes, releasing nutrients back into soil and water. They are decomposers. Some animals, such as earthworms and woodlice, feed on dead organic material and help break it into smaller pieces; these are detritivores. The word “saprophyte” is used in older school texts for organisms that feed on dead organic matter, but “decomposer” is the clearer term for this role.

B. Abiotic (non-living) components
Abiotic components are physical and chemical conditions, including sunlight, temperature, rainfall, water, air, soil, rocks, minerals, salinity, pH and wind. These factors affect which organisms can live in a place and how well they grow.

4. Interdependence in an ecosystem
Living organisms depend on one another for food, pollination, seed dispersal, shelter and population balance. They also depend on non-living components: plants need sunlight, water, carbon dioxide and minerals; animals need water, oxygen and suitable habitats; decomposers need dead organic matter and suitable moisture and temperature.

Non-living components also interact. Rainwater weathers rocks; soil stores water and minerals; temperature affects evaporation; wind moves heat, water vapour and seeds. A change in one component can affect many others. For example, removing trees may expose soil to erosion, increase runoff, reduce habitats and change local water conditions.

5. Food chains and food webs
A food chain shows one pathway through which energy passes from one organism to another. Example:
Grass → grasshopper → frog → snake → hawk.

A food web is a network of connected food chains. Real ecosystems usually contain food webs because most organisms eat more than one type of food and may be eaten by several predators. Energy flows through an ecosystem from sunlight to producers and then to consumers; some energy is lost as heat at each transfer. Matter and nutrients are recycled, but energy is not recycled in the same way.

6. Important cycles that help maintain environmental balance
A. Water cycle
Water evaporates from oceans, rivers, lakes and soil; plants also release water vapour through transpiration. Water vapour cools and condenses to form clouds. Precipitation returns water to land and oceans as rain, snow or hail. Water may flow over the surface as runoff, enter the ground by infiltration, or move underground before returning to rivers and seas.

B. Carbon cycle
Plants take in carbon dioxide during photosynthesis and use carbon to build organic matter. Carbon passes through food chains when organisms eat plants or other organisms. Respiration and decomposition release carbon dioxide. Burning wood and fossil fuels also releases stored carbon to the atmosphere. Oceans, soils and rocks store large amounts of carbon.

C. Nitrogen cycle
Most organisms cannot use nitrogen gas in the air directly. Nitrogen-fixing bacteria and some other natural processes convert it into compounds that can enter the soil and food web. Plants absorb nitrogen mainly as nitrate or ammonium. Animals obtain nitrogen by feeding on plants or other animals. Decomposers return nitrogen from wastes and dead organisms to the soil as ammonium; other bacteria convert nitrogen compounds and may return nitrogen gas to the atmosphere by denitrification.

D. Mineral/nutrient cycle
Weathering releases mineral nutrients from rocks into soil and water. Plants absorb nutrients through their roots. Animals obtain them by eating plants or other animals. When organisms produce waste or die, decomposers return nutrients to the environment, where they can be used again.

7. Environmental balance
Environmental balance is the condition in which the interactions among organisms and their physical surroundings allow an ecosystem to continue functioning. It does not mean that nature never changes. Ecosystems change naturally, but severe or rapid disturbances can reduce biodiversity and disrupt food webs and cycles.

Human activities that can disturb environmental balance include deforestation, pollution, overgrazing, overfishing, habitat destruction, invasive species, excessive use of fertilisers and burning fossil fuels. Conservation, careful resource use, pollution control and habitat protection help reduce these impacts.

8. Answers to the source evaluation and weekend assignment
An ecosystem is a community of organisms interacting with one another and with their non-living environment.
Biotic components are living things; abiotic components are non-living physical and chemical factors.
Plants are producers/autotrophs. Animals and humans are consumers/heterotrophs. Bacteria and fungi are important decomposers.
The water-containing sphere is the hydrosphere. A nutrient/mineral cycle returns nutrients to the environment for reuse. Energy flows through an ecosystem; nutrients are recycled.
Weekend answers: (1) hydrosphere; (2) heterotrophs; (3) ecosystem; (4) autotrophs; (5) mineral/nutrient cycle.
Four importance of the environment include providing air and water, food and raw materials, habitats for organisms, and conditions/resources for human settlement and economic activities.

PRACTICE
1. Define environment and ecosystem. Explain one difference between them.
2. Name the four Earth spheres and give one example of how each supports life.
3. Distinguish biotic and abiotic components, giving four examples of each.
4. Explain the roles of producers, consumers and decomposers in an ecosystem.
5. Draw or describe a food chain with five organisms and explain how it differs from a food web.
6. Describe the main stages of the water cycle.
7. Explain how carbon and nitrogen move through an ecosystem.
8. Explain why nutrients are recycled but energy flows through an ecosystem.
9. State four ways human activities can disturb environmental balance and give two ways to reduce the damage.
10. State four importance of the environment to humans and other organisms.

ANSWER GUIDE
1. Environment is the total living and non-living surroundings; an ecosystem is a community of organisms interacting with one another and with the abiotic environment. Award 2 marks for each definition and 1 for the difference (5 marks).
2. Lithosphere—soil/rocks; hydrosphere—water; atmosphere—air/gases; biosphere—living organisms (4 marks, 1 each).
3. Biotic means living; abiotic means non-living physical/chemical factors (2 marks). Four examples of each (4 marks). Total 6.
4. Producers make organic food; consumers obtain food by eating organisms; decomposers break down dead matter and return nutrients (6 marks, 2 each).
5. Correct five-organism sequence (3 marks); explains energy transfer (1 mark); food web is a network of connected chains (1 mark). Total 5.
6. Evaporation/transpiration, condensation, precipitation, runoff and infiltration/groundwater flow (5 marks).
7. Carbon moves through photosynthesis, feeding, respiration, decomposition and combustion (3 marks). Nitrogen is fixed, absorbed by plants, passed through food webs and returned by decomposition/denitrification (3 marks). Total 6.
8. Nutrients are matter and are returned by decomposition and cycles; energy enters mainly as sunlight, passes through trophic levels and is lost as heat, so it must be continually supplied (3 marks).
9. Any four impacts (4 marks) and two ways to reduce harm (2 marks). Total 6.
10. Any four valid benefits (4 marks).

Total: 50 marks.

SOURCE QUESTION REVIEW
The source describes environmental balance as a continuous supply of energy. The lesson corrects this: energy flows through ecosystems and is lost as heat, while nutrients and matter cycle. The source groups saprophytes under heterotrophs; the lesson distinguishes consumers from decomposers. It also expands the named cycles into student-readable processes, while preserving the source's ecosystem, biotic/abiotic and interdependence objectives.

SOURCES AND PROVENANCE
This is an original SS1 teaching supplement for the school's Second Term Geography Week Five topic. It expands the source's brief definitions and cycle list into a complete ecosystem lesson and corrects the distinction between energy flow and nutrient cycling. The original school document remains unchanged.
U.S. Geological Survey, Water Cycle Processes: https://pubs.usgs.gov/publication/gip235 (evaporation, transpiration, condensation, precipitation and infiltration).
U.S. Geological Survey, Condensation and the Water Cycle: https://www.usgs.gov/water-science-school/science/condensation-and-water-cycle (condensation and precipitation).
NOAA Ocean Service, What is the carbon cycle?: https://oceanservice.noaa.gov/facts/carbon-cycle.html (carbon movement and human impacts).
U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, Ag 101 — Nitrogen: https://www.epa.gov/sites/default/files/2015-07/documents/ag_101_agriculture_us_epa_0.pdf (nitrogen availability and transformations).
U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, Watershed Ecology — Food Webs and Trophic Ecology: https://cfpub.epa.gov/watertrain/pdf/modules/WatershedEcology.pdf (producers, consumers, decomposers and energy flow).

lessons.subject: Geography
lessons.title: Using a map of Nigeria
objectives: Locate Nigeria and identify its neighbouring countries and southern coastline.
State the number of states and identify the FCT as a separate administrative territory.
Identify Abuja as the national capital and distinguish it from state capitals.
Interpret the map legend for capitals, settlements, boundaries, scale and orientation.
Recognise the map's publication date and disclaimer.
lessons.body:
# Using a map of Nigeria

A **locator map** helps us find a country, its neighbours and important places. A political map can also show the states and the Federal Capital Territory.

## 1. Nigeria and its neighbours

Nigeria is in West Africa. The United Nations map shows:
- Benin to the west;
- Niger to the north;
- Chad to the northeast;
- Cameroon to the east and southeast;
- the Gulf of Guinea / Atlantic Ocean to the south.

## 2. States and the Federal Capital Territory

Nigeria has **36 states** and the **Federal Capital Territory (FCT)**. Abuja is the national capital and is located in the FCT.

The United Nations map shows state names, the FCT, major towns and state capitals. It also marks major rivers, Lake Chad, the Niger Delta and the Gulf of Guinea.

## 3. How to read the map

Use the legend:
- A star marks the national capital.
- A filled dot marks a state capital.
- An open circle marks a town or village.
- A dashed line marks an international boundary.
- A dash-dot line marks a state boundary.
- The scale helps estimate distance.
- North is at the top of the map.

## 4. Open the locator map

**United Nations Map of Nigeria, Map No. 4228 Rev. 1 (August 2014):**

https://www.un.org/geospatial/sites/default/files/files/documents/2020/Apr/nigeria_4228_r1_aug14_120.pdf

Open the PDF and use its map and legend while completing the questions. The map shows the 36 states, FCT, capital symbols, neighbouring countries, major rivers and water bodies, scale and orientation.

lessons.subject: Geography
lessons.title: Geographic Information Systems (GIS)
objectives: Define GIS and explain the importance of location-linked information.
Identify and explain the five main components of GIS.
Identify common sources of geographic data and assess basic data quality.
Distinguish spatial data from attribute data.
Distinguish vector and raster data and give examples.
Explain basic GIS functions, uses and limitations.
lessons.body:
GEOGRAPHIC INFORMATION SYSTEMS (GIS)

Learning objectives
By the end of this lesson, you should be able to define GIS, explain its main components, identify common sources of geographic data, distinguish spatial data from attribute data, describe basic GIS data models, and explain practical uses of GIS.

1. Meaning of GIS
A Geographic Information System (GIS) is a computer-based system for collecting, storing, managing, checking, analysing and displaying information linked to places on the Earth's surface. A normal list may tell us how many clinics exist. GIS can show where the clinics are, which communities they serve and which areas are far from a clinic.

The word geographic means that information is connected to a location. The information may use coordinates such as latitude and longitude, a place name, an address or a mapped boundary.

2. Main components of GIS
A working GIS brings together five connected components:
- Hardware: physical equipment such as computers, servers, GPS receivers, scanners, storage devices and printers.
- Software: computer programs used to enter, manage, analyse and display geographic data.
- Data: the location information and the facts linked to each location.
- People: surveyors, geographers, planners, analysts, technicians and decision-makers who collect, manage and interpret the information.
- Methods: the procedures and rules used to collect data, check quality, analyse it and communicate results.

The components work together. A computer without suitable data cannot answer a geographic question; data without trained people and sound methods may be misunderstood.

3. Sources of geographic data
Geographic data can come from:
- Field surveys and direct observation, including measurements made at known locations.
- Global Navigation Satellite Systems (GNSS), including GPS receivers, which provide position observations.
- Aerial photographs and satellite images, which show features from above.
- Existing maps, plans and charts, which may be digitised.
- Census and administrative records, which provide population, household and service information linked to areas.
- Government and scientific datasets, such as roads, rivers, elevation, rainfall and land-cover information.

A dataset should be checked before use. Ask who collected it, when it was collected, what area it covers, what coordinate reference system it uses, how accurate it is and whether its use is permitted.

4. Spatial data and attribute data
Spatial data describe the location, shape or position of a feature. Attribute data describe facts about that feature.

Example: a school may be represented by a point on a map. Its attributes may include the school name, number of classrooms, enrolment and school type. The point tells us where the school is; the table tells us more about it.

5. Basic ways GIS represents geographic features
Vector data represent separate features using:
- Points: features treated as locations, such as a borehole, clinic or school.
- Lines: features with length, such as roads, rivers and pipelines.
- Polygons: closed areas, such as a school compound, local government area or lake boundary.

Raster data represent an area as a grid of cells or pixels. Each cell stores a value. Satellite images, elevation grids and rainfall surfaces are common examples. Raster is useful for continuous information that varies across space; vector is useful for clearly defined individual features and boundaries.

6. What GIS can do
GIS can:
- Display the location of features on a map.
- Search for features that meet a condition.
- Measure distance and area.
- Overlay different layers to examine how features relate.
- Identify areas within a chosen distance of a service.
- Compare mapped information from different dates to study change.

Example: a local authority can combine settlement locations, roads and clinic locations to identify communities that are far from health facilities. The result can help planners decide where further investigation or a new facility may be needed. A map supports a decision; it does not replace field checks or professional judgement.

7. Common uses of GIS
GIS is used in town and regional planning, transport, agriculture, environmental management, disaster response, public health, utilities, natural-resource management and research. In Nigeria, GIS can support mapping of roads, schools, farms, flood-prone areas, health facilities and administrative boundaries.

8. Limitations and responsible use
A GIS map is only as reliable as its data and methods. Old data may not describe current conditions. Inaccurate coordinates can place a feature in the wrong location. Different datasets may use different coordinate reference systems and may not align correctly. Missing data can make an area appear to have no services when the real problem is incomplete reporting. Personal or sensitive location information must be handled responsibly.

Before using a GIS result, check its source, date, scale or resolution, accuracy, coverage and limitations. Never present an estimate as an exact measurement.

PRACTICE
1. Define GIS and explain why location is important in a GIS.
2. List the five main components of GIS and explain the role of any three.
3. State five sources of geographic data.
4. Distinguish spatial data from attribute data using a school as an example.
5. Explain the difference between vector and raster data. Give two examples of each.
6. Describe three ways a local government could use GIS to improve services.
7. State four checks that should be made before relying on a GIS dataset.

ANSWER GUIDE AND MARKING
1. GIS is a computer-based system for collecting, storing, managing, analysing and displaying information linked to locations (3 marks); explains location reference with a suitable example (2 marks). Total 5.
2. Names hardware, software, data, people and methods (5 marks); explains any three correctly (3 marks). Total 8.
3. Any five: field survey/observation, GNSS/GPS, aerial photographs, satellite imagery, existing maps, census/administrative records, government/scientific datasets (5 marks).
4. Spatial data give the school's mapped position/point (2 marks); attribute data give facts such as name, enrolment, classrooms or school type (2 marks). Total 4.
5. Vector uses points, lines and polygons for discrete features (2 marks); raster uses a grid of cells/pixels (2 marks); two suitable examples of each (2 marks). Total 6.
6. Any three explained uses, such as identifying underserved communities, mapping roads and service routes, monitoring land use, locating flood exposure or planning facilities (6 marks).
7. Any four: source/collector, date, geographic coverage, coordinate reference system, accuracy, resolution/scale, completeness and permission to use (4 marks).

Total: 38 marks.

SOURCE ALIGNMENT
The school source's Week Eight heading is “Components of Geographic Information System (GIS)”. Its indexed body names sources of geographic data (lines 459-465) and components of GIS (line 467). This supplement expands those two stated areas into a complete introductory lesson.
